PROLOGUE.
For a long time now I have been thinking about and planning to do what I now

undertake with the Lord's help, since I think it should be put off no longer: to review my little works, whether books, letters or treatises, with a kind of judicial severity, and to mark what displeases me as if with a censor's pen. No one but a fool will dare to find fault with me for finding fault with my own errors. And if he says that I ought not to have said things that later displeased even me, he speaks the truth and takes my side. For he is finding fault with the very things I find fault with. I would not have to find fault with them if I had been right to say them.

But let each person take what I am doing as he pleases. In this matter, at any rate, I had to keep in view the apostle's saying: "If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord." What is written elsewhere also frightens me very much: "In much speaking you will not escape sin." This is not because I have written a great deal, or because many things I said, though not dictated, were nevertheless written down. Far be it from me to call it much speaking when necessary things are said, however many words are used and however long they run. I fear this saying of holy Scripture because, from so many discussions of mine, many things could no doubt be gathered which, even if not false, would certainly seem unnecessary, or might even be shown to be so. And which of his faithful has Christ not frightened by saying: "For every idle word that a man speaks, he will give account of it on the day of judgment"? So too his apostle James says: "Let every man be quick to hear but slow to speak"; and in another place: "Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you receive a greater judgment. For we all offend in many things. If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man." I do not claim this perfection for myself even now that I am old; how much less when I began as a young man to write or to speak to the people. So much was granted to me that wherever I was present and someone had to address the people, I was very rarely allowed to keep silent, listen to others, and be quick to hear but slow to speak. It remains, then, for me to judge myself under the one Teacher, whose judgment on my offenses I wish to escape. I think people become many teachers when they hold different views that conflict with one another. But when they all say the same thing and say what is true, they do not depart from the teaching of the one true Teacher. They offend, not when they say much that is his, but when they add their own. For in this way, from much speaking, they fall into false speaking too.

I have decided to write this so that I may put it into the hands of people from whom I cannot recall the works I have already published in order to correct them. Nor do I pass over the things I wrote while still a catechumen, when I had indeed abandoned the earthly hope I once cherished but was still puffed up by my habit of secular literature. For these too came to the notice of copyists and readers, and they can be read with profit if some things are pardoned, or, if they are not pardoned, provided that no one clings to their errors. So whoever is going to read these works, let him not imitate me in my errors but in my progress toward the better. For anyone who reads my little works in the order in which they were written will perhaps discover how I made progress by writing. To make this possible, I will take care in this work, as far as I can, that he may know that order.
CHAPTER I. ON THE ACADEMICS, THREE BOOKS.

When I had left behind both what I had gained and what I still wished to gain among the desires of this world, and had withdrawn to the leisure of the Christian life, I wrote first, before I was baptized, against the Academics, or on the Academics. My aim was to drive from my mind, with all the arguments I could muster, their reasonings, which make many people despair of finding the truth, forbid the wise man to assent to anything or to approve anything at all as though it were plain and certain, since everything seems obscure and uncertain to them. I did this because those reasonings troubled me. And by the Lord's mercy and help it was done.

But in those three books I am displeased that I so often spoke of fortune, though I did not mean any goddess to be understood by that name, but the chance outcome of events, whether in the goods or evils of our body or in external things. Hence come words that no religion forbids us to use: "by chance," "perhaps," "perchance," "maybe," "fortuitously." Yet all this must be referred back to divine providence. I did not keep silent about this there either, saying: "For perhaps what is commonly called fortune is governed by some hidden order, and what we call chance in events is nothing but that whose reason and cause are hidden." I did say this, yet I regret having named fortune there as I did, since I see that people have the very bad habit of saying "Fortune willed this" where they ought to say "God willed this."

Again, where I said in one place: "It is so ordained, whether because of our deserts or by necessity of nature, that the harbor of philosophy by no means receives the divine mind while it clings to mortal things," and so on, either I should have said neither of these two things, since the sense could be complete even so, or it would have been enough to say "because of our deserts," as is true of the misery derived from Adam, without adding "or by necessity of nature," since the harsh necessity of our nature arose from the desert of earlier wickedness.

Likewise, where I said there that "nothing at all is to be worshiped, and everything is to be cast aside that is seen by mortal eyes or that any sense touches," words should have been added so as to say "whatever the sense of the mortal body touches," for there is also a sense of the mind. But at that time I was speaking in the manner of those who call sense only that of the body, and sensible things only bodily things. So wherever I have spoken this way, ambiguity has not been sufficiently avoided, except for those who are used to this way of speaking. I also said:

"What do you think living happily is, other than living according to what is best in man?" And a little later I explained what I meant by what is best in man: "Who," I said, "would doubt that what is best in man is nothing other than that part of the soul to whose rule everything else in man ought to submit? This, so that you do not ask for another definition, may be called mind or reason." This is indeed true, for as far as human nature goes, there is nothing better in man than mind and reason. But whoever wishes to live happily ought not to live according to it. Otherwise he lives according to man, when he should live according to God in order to reach happiness. To attain it, our mind must not be content with itself but must be subject to God.

Likewise, answering the one with whom I was debating, I said: "Here you are plainly not mistaken, and I would gladly wish this to be an omen for you for the rest." Although this was said in jest and not seriously, I would still rather not have used that word. I do not remember reading "omen" either in our sacred writings or in the speech of any churchly disputant, although "abomination," which is found constantly in the divine books, gets its name from it.

In the second book, that fable, so to speak, about philocalia and philosophy, that they are sisters born of the same parent, is utterly silly and tasteless. For either what is called philocalia lies only in trifles, and so is in no sense a sister of philosophy; or, if the name deserves honor because in Latin translation it means the love of beauty, and the true and highest beauty is that of wisdom, then in incorporeal and supreme things philocalia is the very same as philosophy, and they are in no way two sisters, as it were.

In another place, while discussing the soul, I said: "more safely about to return to heaven." I would have spoken more safely had I said "to go" rather than "to return," because of those who think that human souls fell or were cast down from heaven for the deserts of their sins and thrust into these bodies. But I did not hesitate to say it, because I said "to heaven" as if I were saying "to God," who is its author and maker, just as blessed Cyprian did not hesitate to say: "For since we have the body from earth and the spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven." And in the book of Ecclesiastes it is written: "Let the spirit return to God, who gave it." This must of course be understood so as not to contradict the apostle, who says that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil. Beyond dispute, then, God himself is a kind of original homeland of the soul's happiness. He did not beget it from himself, but neither did he make it from anything else, as he made the body from earth. As for its origin, by which it comes to be in the body, whether it comes from that one man who was created first, when man was made a living soul, or whether individual souls are made in the same way for individual people, I did not know then and I do not know now.

In the third book: "If you ask what I think," I said, "I believe that man's highest good lies in the mind." I would have spoken more truly had I said "in God," for the mind enjoys him as its highest good in order to be happy.
Nor am I pleased that I said: "I may freely swear by everything divine."

Likewise, what I said of the Academics, that they knew the truth, whose likeness they called the truth-like, and that I called this very truth-like thing, which they approved, false, was wrongly said for two reasons. First, because what was in some way like a truth would not be false, since in its own kind it too is true. Second, because I said they approved these false things which they called truth-like, when they approved nothing and asserted that the wise man approves nothing. But since they also called this truth-like thing the probable, that is how I came to say this of them.

The praise, too, with which I extolled Plato and the Platonists, or the Academic philosophers, more than was fitting for ungodly men, has rightly displeased me, especially since Christian teaching must be defended against their great errors.

Also, when I compared Cicero's arguments, which he used in his Academic books, with my own and called mine trifles, though I refuted those arguments with the most certain reasoning, I ought not to have said it, even though it was said in jest and more by way of irony.
This work begins: "O would that, Romanianus, a man fitted to himself."
CHAPTER II. ON THE HAPPY LIFE, ONE BOOK.

It so happened that I wrote the book On the Happy Life not after the books On the Academics but between them. It arose on the occasion of my birthday and was completed in a discussion lasting three days, as the book itself makes clear enough. In it, we who were inquiring together agreed that the happy life is nothing other than the perfect knowledge of God.
What displeases me there is that I attributed more to Mallius Theodorus, to whom I wrote the book, learned and Christian man though he was,
than I should have; and that there too I often spoke of fortune;

and that I said that in the time of this life the happy life dwells in the mind of the wise man alone, whatever the state of his body. For the apostle hopes for the perfect knowledge of God, that is, the greatest that a human being can have, in the life to come, which alone deserves to be called the happy life, where the body too, incorruptible and immortal, will be subject to its spirit without any trouble or resistance. I did indeed find this book in our copy broken off and missing no small part, and it was copied that way by some of the brothers. Nor had I yet found a complete copy anywhere from which to correct it when I was revising these works.
This book begins: "If to the harbor of philosophy."
CHAPTER III. ON ORDER, TWO BOOKS.

At the same time, in between the books written on the Academics, I also wrote two books On Order. They deal with a great question: whether the order of divine providence embraces all things, good and evil. But when I saw that the matter was hard to understand and could only with great difficulty be brought within the grasp of those I was debating with, I preferred to speak about the order of study, by which one can advance from bodily things to incorporeal ones.
But in these books too I am displeased by the frequent insertion of the word "fortune"; and that I did not add
"of the body" when I spoke of the bodily senses;
and that I attributed much to the liberal disciplines, of which many saints know very little, while some who know them are not saints;
and that I mentioned the Muses as if they were some sort of goddesses, even though in jest; and that I called wonder a vice;
and that I said that philosophers not endowed with true piety had shone with the light of virtue;

and that I commended the idea of two worlds, one sensible and the other intelligible, not as the view of Plato or the Platonists but as my own, as if the Lord too had meant to indicate this, since he did not say, "My kingdom is not of the world," but, "My kingdom is not of this world." Yet this may be found to be simply a manner of speaking; and if another world is meant by Christ the Lord, it can more fittingly be understood as the one in which there will be a new heaven and a new earth, when what we pray for in saying "Your kingdom come" is fulfilled. Nor was Plato mistaken in saying that there is an intelligible world, if we are willing to attend not to the word, which is unusual for this matter in the Church's usage, but to the thing itself. For he called the intelligible world the eternal and unchangeable reason by which God made the world. Whoever denies that this exists must say that God made what he made without reason, or that when he was making it, or before he made it, he did not know what he was making, if he had no reason for making it. But if he had one, as he did, it seems that Plato called this the intelligible world. Still, we would not use that term if we were already well enough versed in the Church's writings.

Nor am I pleased that, after saying, "The greatest effort must be given to the best morals," I added straightaway: "for otherwise our God will not be able to hear us, but those who live well he will hear most readily." This was said as though God does not hear sinners. That was indeed said in the Gospel, but by one who did not yet know Christ, though Christ had already given light to his bodily eyes.

Nor am I pleased that I gave so much praise to the philosopher Pythagoras that anyone who hears or reads it might think I believed there were no errors in Pythagorean doctrine, when there are many, and grave ones.
This work begins: "On the order of things, Zenobius."
CHAPTER IV. SOLILOQUIES, TWO BOOKS.

Meanwhile I also wrote two volumes, following my own desire and love of tracking down the truth by reason about the things I most longed to know. I questioned myself and answered myself as if we were two, reason and I, although I was alone. So I called this work the Soliloquies. But it remained unfinished. Even so, the first book asks, and shows in some fashion, what sort of person someone must be who wishes to grasp wisdom, which is grasped by the mind and not by the bodily senses. At the end of that book a line of reasoning reaches the conclusion that the things which truly exist are immortal. In the second book the immortality of the soul is discussed at length, but the discussion is not brought to a conclusion.

In these books I certainly do not approve of what I said in the prayer: "God, who willed that none but the pure should know the truth." For one could reply that many who are not pure also know many true things. Nor is it defined there what the truth is that none but the pure can know, or what knowing is.

Then there is the statement made there: "God, whose kingdom is the whole world, which sense does not know." If this is to be understood of God, some words should have been added, so that it read: "which the sense of the mortal body does not know." If, on the other hand, it is the world that is said to be unknown to sense, then it is rightly understood as the world that is to come, with a new heaven and a new earth. But here too those words should have been added, so that it read: "the sense of the mortal body." At that time, however, I was still speaking in the manner in which the word "sense" properly refers to the body. I need not keep repeating what I have already said about this above, but it should be borne in mind wherever this expression is found in my writings.
And where I said of the Father and the Son, "He who begets and he whom he begets is one," I ought to have said "are one," as the Truth himself plainly says: "I and the Father are one."
Nor am I pleased with my statement that in this life the soul is already happy once it has understood God, unless perhaps in hope.

Again, my statement that "one reaches union with wisdom by more than one way" does not sound right, as if there were some other way besides Christ, who said, "I am the way." I should therefore have avoided giving this offense to religious ears. Granted, there is that one universal way, and there are also other ways, of which we sing in the Psalm: "Make your ways known to me, Lord, and teach me your paths."

Where it is said there that "these sensible things are to be fled from utterly," I should have taken care not to be thought to hold the opinion of Porphyry, that false philosopher, who said that every body is to be fled from. I did not say "all sensible things," however, but "these," that is, corruptible ones. But I should rather have said this, for there will be no such sensible things in the new heaven and new earth of the age to come.

Again, in one passage I said that those who are trained in the liberal disciplines undoubtedly draw them out by learning, buried in oblivion within themselves, and in a sense dig them up again. But I disapprove of this too. It is more credible that even people unskilled in certain disciplines give true answers about them when they are questioned well because the light of eternal reason is present to them, so far as they can take it in, and in that light they behold these unchangeable truths. It is not because they once knew them and have forgotten them, as Plato and others like him thought. I argued against their opinion in the twelfth book of On the Trinity, as far as the occasion allowed in the work I had undertaken.
This work begins: "When I had long been turning over many and various things in my mind."
CHAPTER 5. ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, ONE BOOK.

After the books of the Soliloquies, and after I had returned from the country to Milan, I wrote a book on the immortality of the soul. I had meant it to be a kind of memorandum for myself to help me finish the Soliloquies, which had remained incomplete. But somehow, against my will, it got into people's hands and is listed among my minor works. First of all, it is so obscure because its reasoning is tangled and compressed that it wearies even my own attention when I read it, and I can scarcely understand it myself.

Then, because I was thinking of nothing but human minds, I said in one argument of that book: "Nor can learning exist in one who learns nothing." Likewise I said in another passage: "Nor does knowledge embrace anything except what belongs to some discipline." It did not occur to me that God does not learn disciplines and yet has knowledge of all things, including foreknowledge of the future. Of the same kind is the statement made there that no one has life with reason except a soul. For God does not have life without reason, since in him are both the highest life and the highest reason. And a little earlier I said that what is understood always remains as it is, although the mind too is understood, and the mind certainly does not always remain as it is. As for my statement that the mind cannot be separated from eternal reason because it is not joined to it spatially, I would surely not have said this if I had then been so well versed in the sacred writings as to recall what is written: "Your sins separate you from God." From this we are given to understand that one can also speak of the separation of things that were joined not in space but in an incorporeal way.

I have also been unable to remember what I meant when I said: "If the soul lacks a body, it is not in this world." Do the souls of the dead not lack a body, or are they not in this world? As if the underworld were not in this world! But since lacking a body can be a good thing, perhaps by the word "body" I meant bodily afflictions. If so, I used the word in a very unusual way.

This too was said rashly: that form is bestowed on the body by the supreme being through the soul, and by this form the body exists to whatever extent it exists. So, it said, the body subsists through the soul and exists by the very fact that it is animated, whether universally, as the world is, or individually, as each animal within the world is. All of this was said quite rashly.
This book begins: "If there is learning anywhere."

During the same period, while I was in Milan about to receive baptism, I also tried to write books on the disciplines. I questioned those who were with me and who had no aversion to such studies, wishing to reach, or to lead others to, incorporeal things through corporeal ones, by sure steps, as it were. But of these I managed to complete only the book on grammar, which I later lost from our book chest, and six volumes on music, as far as concerns the part of music called rhythm. I wrote those six books, however, after I had been baptized and had returned from Italy to Africa; in Milan I had only begun that discipline. Of the other five disciplines, likewise begun there, namely dialectic, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic and philosophy, only the opening sections remained. We have lost even these, but I believe some people have copies.
CHAPTER 6.
ON THE MORALS OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH AND ON THE MORALS OF THE MANICHAEANS, TWO BOOKS.

Once I had been baptized, while I was in Rome, I could not bear in silence the Manichaeans' boasting about their false and deceitful continence or abstinence. To deceive the unlearned, they even set themselves above true Christians, with whom they are not to be compared. So I wrote two books, one on the morals of the Catholic Church and the other on the morals of the Manichaeans.

In the book on the morals of the Catholic Church I quoted a text that reads: "For your sake we are afflicted all day long; we are regarded as sheep." There an error in our manuscript misled me, since I did not remember the scriptures well, not yet being familiar with them. Other manuscripts of the same translation do not read "for your sake we are afflicted" but "for your sake we are put to death," which others have rendered with a single word, "we are being killed." The Greek books show that this is the truer reading. It was from Greek that the ancient divine scriptures were translated into Latin, following the Septuagint translators. Nevertheless, I said a great deal on the basis of those words, "for your sake we are afflicted." I do not reject what I said as false in substance, but I certainly did not demonstrate from these words, at least, the agreement between the old and new scriptures that I wished to show. I have explained how the error crept in on me; but I showed that same agreement adequately from other testimonies.

A little later I quoted a text from the book of Wisdom as it stood in our manuscript, where it was written: "For wisdom teaches sobriety and justice and virtue." On the basis of these words I discussed things that are indeed true, but that were discovered by occasion of a copying error. For what is truer than that wisdom teaches the truth of contemplation, which I took to be signified by the word "sobriety," and uprightness of action, which I meant to be understood by the other two words, justice and virtue? Yet the more accurate manuscripts of the same translation read: "For it teaches sobriety and wisdom and justice and virtue." With all these words the Latin translator named those four virtues which are so often on the lips of philosophers. He called temperance "sobriety," gave prudence the name "wisdom," and expressed fortitude with the word "virtue"; only justice did he translate by its own name. Long afterward we found in Greek manuscripts that in this same book of Wisdom these four virtues are called by their proper names, as the Greeks call them.

Likewise, the text I quoted from the book of Solomon, "Vanity of the vain, said Ecclesiastes" (vanitantium), I had indeed read in many manuscripts. But the Greek does not have this; it has "vanity of vanities" (vanitatum), as I later saw. And I found that the Latin manuscripts reading "of vanities" rather than "of the vain" are the more accurate. Still, whatever I discussed by occasion of this copying error is evidently true in substance.

Where I said, "Let us first love with full charity the very one we wish to know, that is, God," it would have been better to say "sincere" rather than "full." Otherwise one might think that our love for God will not be greater when we see him face to face. So let it be taken as if "full" meant a love that cannot be greater as long as we walk by faith. For it will be fuller, indeed fullest, but by sight.

Again, I said of those who help the needy that they are called merciful even if they are so wise that they are no longer troubled by any distress of mind. This is not to be taken as if I had asserted that there are such wise people in this life. For I did not say "since they are," but "even if they are."

In another passage I said: "Now, when this human love has nourished and strengthened the soul that clings to its breasts, the soul becomes fit to follow God. When his majesty begins to disclose itself, as far as suffices for the soul while it dwells on this earth, there arises such an ardor of charity and there blazes up such a fire of divine love that, once all vices have been burned away in a person sanctified and cleansed, it becomes plain how divinely it was said: 'I am a consuming fire.'" The Pelagians may think that I said this perfection can be attained in this mortal life. But let them not think so. For the ardor of charity that has become fit to follow God, and is so great that it consumes all vices, can be born and can grow in this life. But it cannot accordingly achieve here the purpose for which it is born, namely that no vice should remain in a person. Yet so great a thing is accomplished by that same ardor of charity, where and when it can be accomplished. Just as the washing of regeneration cleanses from the guilt of all the sins that human birth brought with it and human wickedness added, so that perfection will cleanse from the stain of all the vices without which human weakness cannot exist in this world. This is also how we must take what the apostle said: "Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so as to present the church to himself in glory, without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind." For here is the washing of water in the word, by which the church is cleansed. But since the whole church says, as long as it is here, "Forgive us our debts," it certainly is not here without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind. Yet from what it receives here it is led on to that glory and perfection which is not found here.
In the other book, entitled On the Morals of the Manichaeans,

I said: "The goodness of God so orders all things that fall away that they are where they can most fittingly be, until by ordered movements they return to that from which they fell away." This is not to be taken as if all things return to that from which they fell away, as Origen thought, but rather all those that do return. For those who will be punished with everlasting fire will not return to God, from whom they fell away. Even so, all things that fall away are so ordered as to be where they can most fittingly be, since those who do not return are also most fittingly placed in punishment.

In another passage I said: "Hardly anyone doubts that beetles come into being from dung that they have rolled into a ball and buried." But many doubt whether this example is true, and many have not even heard of it.
This work begins: "In other books, I think, we have dealt sufficiently."
CHAPTER 7.
ON THE GREATNESS OF THE SOUL, ONE BOOK.

In the same city I wrote a dialogue in which many questions about the soul are raised and discussed: where it comes from, what it is like, how great it is, why it was given to the body, what it becomes when it comes to the body, and what it becomes when it departs. But the question of how great it is was argued most carefully and subtly, so as to show, if we could, that the soul has no bodily magnitude and yet is something great. So the whole book took its name from this one inquiry and was called On the Greatness of the Soul.

In that book I said that I thought the soul had brought all the arts with it, and that what is called learning is nothing other than remembering and recollecting. This is not to be taken as if it proved that the soul once lived either in another body or somewhere else, whether in a body or outside one, and that the answers it gives when questioned, though it did not learn them here, it learned earlier in another life. For it may be, as we have already said above in this work, that the soul can do this because it is by nature intelligible and is connected not only with intelligible things but also with unchangeable ones. It was made in such an order that when it turns toward the things with which it is connected, or toward itself, it gives true answers about them to the extent that it sees them. Nor, indeed, did it bring all the arts with it in this way or possess them in itself. For about the arts that concern the bodily senses, such as much of medicine and all of astrology, it can say nothing except what it has learned here. But it answers about the things that understanding alone grasps, for the reason I have given, when it has been well questioned and has remembered, whether by itself or by another.

In another passage I said: "I should like to say more on this point and to bind myself, while I am as it were instructing you, to do nothing else than to be restored to myself, to whom I most owe myself." Here it seems that I ought rather to have said: "to be restored to God, to whom I most owe myself." But I spoke as I did because a person must first be restored to himself, so that from there, as from a step, he may rise and be lifted up to God. So the younger son first came to himself and then said, "I will arise and go to my father." Indeed, I added immediately: "and so to become the Lord's friendly bondservant." So when I said "to whom I most owe myself," I was making a comparison with other people. For I owe myself more to myself than to other people, though I owe myself more to God than to myself.
This book begins: "Since I see that you have abundant leisure."
CHAPTER 8.
ON FREE CHOICE, THREE BOOKS.

While we were still staying in Rome, we wished [?] to investigate by discussion where evil comes from. We conducted the discussion so that, if we could, careful and thorough reasoning would lead us to understand, as far as we could manage through discussion with God's help, what we already believed on this matter in submission to divine authority. And since it became clear between us, after careful examination by reason, that evil arises only from the free choice of the will, the three books that this discussion produced were called On Free Choice. I finished the second and third of these in Africa, as well as I could at the time, after I had been ordained a priest at Hippo Regius.

So many matters were discussed in these books that certain questions arose which I either could not unravel or which would have needed a long discussion at the time. These were put aside in such a way that, whichever side of these questions, or whichever of their several aspects, might better agree with the truth (and this was not clear), our reasoning still reached one conclusion: whichever of them was true, God would be believed, or even shown, to deserve praise. That discussion was undertaken because of those who deny that evil originates in the free choice of the will, and who argue that if it does, then God, the creator of all natures, must be blamed. In this way, following the error of their impiety (for they are Manichees), they seek to bring in an unchangeable nature of evil, coeternal with God. But nothing was discussed in these books about the grace of God, by which he has so predestined his elect that he himself also prepares the wills of those among them who already use free choice, because that was not the question proposed. Where there was occasion to mention this grace, it was mentioned in passing. It was not defended with laborious reasoning, as if it were the subject in hand. For it is one thing to ask where evil comes from, and another to ask how one returns to the original good or attains a greater one.

So the new heretics, the Pelagians, should not exalt themselves as though I had pleaded their cause. They assert free choice of the will in such a way that they leave no room for the grace of God, since they claim that it is given according to our merits. It is true that I said a great deal in these books in favor of free choice, but that was because the purpose of the discussion required it. In the first book I said that evil deeds are punished by the justice of God, and I added: "For they would not be justly punished unless they were done by the will." Again, when I was showing that a good will is so great a good that it is rightly preferred to all bodily and external goods, I said: "So you see now, I think, that it lies in our will whether we enjoy or lack so great and so true a good. For what lies so much in the will as the will itself?" And in another place: "What reason is there, then," I said, "for us to think we should doubt that, even if we were never wise before, it is still by the will that we merit and lead a praiseworthy and happy life, and by the will a shameful and wretched one?" And again in another place: "From this it follows," I said, "that whoever wishes to live rightly and honorably, if he wishes this above fleeting things, attains so great a thing with such ease that for him, to have what he willed is nothing other than to will it." And elsewhere I said: "For that eternal law, which it is now time to return to and consider, has established with unchangeable firmness that merit lies in the will, while reward and punishment lie in happiness and misery." And in another place: "It has been established," I said, "that what each person chooses to pursue and embrace lies in the will." And in the second book: "For a human being himself," I said, "insofar as he is a human being, is a good, because he can live rightly when he wills." And in another place I said that right action is not possible except by that same free choice of the will. And in the third book: "What need is there," I said, "to ask where this movement comes from, by which the will turns away from the unchangeable good to a changeable good, since we acknowledge that it belongs only to the soul, that it is voluntary, and for that reason blameworthy? All useful teaching on this matter serves this purpose: that, having condemned and restrained this movement, we may turn our will from its fall into temporal things to the enjoyment of the everlasting good." And in another place: "The truth," I said, "cries out from you, though obscurely. For you could not perceive anything to be in our power except what we do when we will. So nothing is so much in our power as the will itself, for it is at hand at once, without any interval, as soon as we will." Again in another place: "For if you are praised," I said, "for seeing what you ought to do, though you see it only in him who is unchangeable truth, how much more is he to be praised who both commanded us to will, and gave us the power, and did not allow us to refuse with impunity." Then I added: "For if each person owes what he has received, and man was made in such a way that he sins of necessity, then what he owes is to sin. So when he sins, he does what he ought. But if it is wicked to say this, then no one is forced by his own nature to sin." And again: "What, after all," I said, "could be the cause of the will before the will? Either it is itself a will, and we do not depart from this root, the will; or it is not a will, and then it has no sin. So either the will is the first cause of sinning, or no sin is the first cause of sinning. Nor is there anyone to whom sin can be imputed except the sinner. It can therefore rightly be imputed to nothing but the will." And a little later: "Who," I said, "sins in something that he can in no way avoid? But sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided." Pelagius used this statement of mine in one of his books. When I replied to that book, I chose to give mine the title On Nature and Grace.

In these and similar words of mine the grace of God is not mentioned, because it was not then the subject, and so the Pelagians think, or may think, that we held their view. But they think so in vain. The will is what we sin by and what we live rightly by, and that is what I was dealing with in these words. Yet unless this will is freed by the grace of God from the slavery by which it has become the slave of sin, and is helped to overcome its vices, mortals cannot live rightly and devoutly. And unless this divine gift by which it is set free came before the will, it would be given for the will's merits, and it would not be grace, which is certainly given freely. We have dealt with this sufficiently in other works of ours, in which we refute these enemies of grace, the new heretics. Even in these books on free choice, which were not written against them at all (they did not yet exist) but against the Manichees, we were not entirely silent about this grace of God, which they try to take away with abominable impiety. In the second book we said that not only great goods but even the least goods cannot exist except from him from whom all good things come, that is, God. And a little later: "The virtues," I said, "by which one lives rightly, are great goods. The beauty of any bodies, without which one can live rightly, is among the least goods. The powers of the soul, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods. No one uses the virtues badly, but anyone can use the other goods, the intermediate and the least, not only well but also badly. And no one uses virtue badly because the work of virtue is the good use of those things that we can also use badly; and no one uses something badly by using it well. So the abundance and greatness of God's goodness has provided not only great goods but also intermediate and least goods. His goodness is more to be praised in the great goods than in the intermediate, and more in the intermediate than in the least. But it is more to be praised in all of them together than if he had not given them all." And in another place: "Only hold fast to an unshaken devotion," I said, "so that no good may present itself to you, whether you perceive it by the senses, understand it, or think of it in any way, that is not from God." And again in another place I said: "But since man cannot rise of his own accord as he fell of his own accord, let us hold with firm faith to the right hand of God stretched out to us from above, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ."

In the third book, after saying what I mentioned Pelagius had taken from my works ("For who sins in something that he can in no way avoid? But sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided"), I went straight on to add: "And yet some things done even through ignorance are condemned and judged to need correction, as we read in the divine authorities. For the apostle says, 'I obtained mercy, because I acted in ignorance'; and the prophet says, 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and of my ignorance.' There are also things done from necessity that must be condemned, when a man wants to do right and cannot. Otherwise, where do these words come from: 'I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, that I do'; and this: 'To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not'; and this: 'The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want'? But all these belong to people who come from that condemnation to death. For if this is not man's punishment but his nature, then none of these things are sins. For if he does not depart from the way he was naturally made, such that he cannot be better, then when he does these things he does what he ought. But if man were good, he would be otherwise. As it is, because he is like this, he is not good, nor is it in his power to be good, either because he does not see what he ought to be, or because he sees it and is not able to be what he sees he ought to be. Who would doubt that this is a punishment? Every punishment, if it is just, is a punishment for sin and is called a penalty. But if it is an unjust punishment (and no one doubts that it is a punishment), then it was imposed on man by some unjust ruler. Now since it is madness to doubt the omnipotence and justice of God, this punishment is just and is paid for some sin. For no unjust ruler could have stolen man away as though God did not know, or wrested him from God against his will as though God were weaker, whether by frightening or by confounding him, so as to torment man with an unjust punishment. It remains, then, that this just punishment comes from the condemnation of man." And in another place: "To approve falsehoods as truths," I said, "so as to err unwillingly, and to be unable to refrain from lustful acts because the pain of the fleshly bond resists and torments us, is not the nature of man as he was created but the punishment of man as condemned. When we speak of the will that is free to do right, we are speaking, of course, of the will in which man was made."

See how long before the Pelagian heresy appeared we argued as though we were already arguing against them. When all goods were said to come from God (the great, the intermediate and the least), free choice of the will was found among the intermediate goods, because we can also use it badly. Yet it is such that without it we cannot live rightly. The good use of it, however, is already virtue, which is found among the great goods, which no one can use badly. And since all goods, as has been said, great, intermediate and least, are from God, it follows that the good use of free will, which is virtue and is counted among the great goods, is also from God. Then it was said from what misery, most justly inflicted on sinners, the grace of God sets us free, because man was able to fall of his own accord, that is, by free choice, but not also to rise. To this misery of just condemnation belong the ignorance and difficulty that every human being suffers from the beginning of his birth, and no one is freed from this evil except by the grace of God. The Pelagians refuse to accept that this misery comes from a just condemnation, since they deny original sin. Yet even if ignorance and difficulty were man's natural original condition, God would still not deserve blame but praise, as we argued in that same third book. That argument must be used against the Manichees, who do not accept the holy scriptures of the Old Testament, in which original sin is narrated, and who contend with detestable shamelessness that whatever is read on this subject in the apostolic writings was inserted by corrupters of the scriptures, as though the apostles had not said it. But against the Pelagians we must defend what both Testaments teach, since they profess to accept both.
This work begins: "Tell me, please, whether God is not the author of evil."
CHAPTER 9. TWO BOOKS ON GENESIS AGAINST THE MANICHEES.

Once I had settled in Africa, I wrote two books on Genesis against the Manichees. In all the arguments of my earlier books I showed that God is the supremely good and unchangeable creator of all changeable natures, and that no nature or substance is evil insofar as it is a nature and substance. In this my aim was always directed against the Manichees. But these two books were published quite openly against them, in defense of the Old Law, which they attack with the violent zeal of their insane error. The first covers the text from "In the beginning God made heaven and earth" until the seven days are completed, where we read that God rested on the seventh day. The second covers the text from "This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth" until Adam and his wife were sent out of paradise and a guard was set over the tree of life. Then, at the end of the book, I set the faith of catholic truth against the error of the Manichees, summing up briefly and clearly what they say and what we say.

I said: "That light does not feed the eyes of irrational birds, but the pure hearts of those who believe God and turn from love of visible and temporal things to fulfilling his commandments, which all men can do if they will." The new heretics, the Pelagians, should not think that this was said in their sense. For it is entirely true that all men can do this if they will. But the will is prepared by the Lord, and it is so strengthened by the gift of charity that they are able to. This was not said here because it was not necessary for the question at hand.

In that work one reads that the Lord's blessing, of which it is said "Increase and multiply," should be believed to have been turned into fleshly fruitfulness after sin. If this cannot be taken to mean anything other than that those first humans would not have had human children if they had not sinned, I do not approve of it at all.

Nor does it follow that we must take it only as allegory that in Genesis green plants and fruit-bearing trees are given as food to every kind of beast and to all birds and all serpents, on the ground that there are four-footed creatures and birds that seem to live on flesh alone. For it could have been that these were fed by humans on the fruits of the earth as well, if, because of the obedience in which humans served God without any wickedness, they had deserved to have all beasts and birds wholly subject to them.

Again, someone may be troubled by how I said of the people of Israel: "That people still served the law through bodily circumcision and sacrifices, as if in the sea of the Gentiles." For among the Gentiles they could not offer sacrifice, just as we see that even now they have remained without sacrifices, unless perhaps the sheep they slaughter at Passover is counted as a sacrifice.
In the second book too, what I put forward, that by the word "fodder"

life can be signified, does not seem to have been said aptly enough, for the manuscripts with the better translation do not have "fodder" but "hay." And the word "hay" does not fit the meaning of life as "fodder" does. Again, I do not seem to have been right to call prophetic the words in which it is written, "Why is earth and ashes proud?" for they are not found in a book that we are certain should be called a prophet.

Nor, when I was explaining the text "God breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul" (or "a soul that lives"), did I understand the apostle as he wished to be understood when he cites this testimony from Genesis, saying, "The first man Adam became a living soul." For the apostle used this testimony to prove that there is an animal body. But I thought it should be used to show that the first man was made animal, not just the man's body.

I said that no nature is harmed by any sins but its own. I said this because whoever harms a righteous person does not truly harm him, since he increases his reward in heaven; but by sinning he truly harms himself, since because of his very will to harm he will receive back the harm he did. The Pelagians may, of course, drag this statement into support of their doctrine and say that infants have not been harmed by the sins of others, since I said that no nature is harmed by any sins but its own. But they fail to see that infants, who certainly belong to human nature, contract original sin precisely because human nature sinned in the first humans; and so human nature has been harmed by no sins but its own. For through one man, in whom all sinned, sin entered the world. I did not say that no human being is harmed by any sins but his own, but that no nature is.

Again, in what I said a little later, that there is no natural evil, they may look for a similar hiding place, unless this statement is referred to nature as it was originally created without fault. That is what is truly and properly called man's nature. But we use the word in a transferred sense when we also call "nature" the state in which man is born. In this sense the apostle said, "For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest."
This work begins: "If the Manichees chose whom to deceive."
CHAPTER 10.
SIX BOOKS ON MUSIC.

Then, as I mentioned above, I wrote six books on music. The sixth of these became especially well known, because it deals with a subject worth knowing: how one may advance from bodily and spiritual numbers, which are changeable, to unchangeable numbers, which already exist in unchangeable truth itself, and so the invisible things of God may be understood and seen through the things that have been made. Those who cannot do this, but still live by faith in Christ, come to see these things more surely and more happily after this life. But those who can do it, if they lack faith in Christ, the one mediator between God and men, perish with all their wisdom.

In this book I said: "For bodies are better the more they abound in such numbers, whereas the soul becomes better by doing without those numbers which it receives through the body, when it turns away from the carnal senses and is re-formed by the divine numbers of wisdom." This is not to be taken as if there will be no bodily numbers in incorruptible and spiritual bodies, since those bodies will be more beautiful and more seemly. Nor does it mean that the soul will not perceive these numbers when it is at its best, just because here it becomes better by doing without them. For here the soul needs to turn away from the carnal senses in order to grasp intelligible things, because it is weak and not well able to direct its attention to both at once. At present, too, we must guard against the allurement of these bodily things for as long as the soul can be lured into shameful delight. Then, however, the soul will be strong and perfect. Bodily numbers will not draw it away from the contemplation of wisdom, and it will perceive them without being enticed by them or made better by doing without them. It will be so good and upright that they can neither escape its notice nor take possession of it.

I also said: "This health, however, will be most firm and most certain when this body has been restored to its original stability at its own fixed time and in its own order." This should not be thought to mean that bodies after the resurrection will be no better than the bodies of the first human beings in paradise, for the risen bodies will no longer need the bodily food that nourished those first bodies. "Original stability" is to be understood only in this sense: those bodies will suffer no sickness at all, just as these bodies could not have suffered any before sin.

In another place I said: "The love of this world is more toilsome. For what the soul seeks in it, namely constancy and eternity, it does not find, since the lowest beauty is made complete by the passing away of things, and whatever in it imitates constancy is passed on from the supreme God through the soul. For the form that is changeable only in time comes before the form that is changeable both in time and in place." These words can be taken to mean that the lowest beauty is found only in the bodies of human beings and of all the animals, which we live among by bodily sense. Understood in that way, they are defended by plain reason. For what imitates constancy in that beauty is that the same bodies hold together in their structure, insofar as they do hold together, and this is passed on to them from the supreme God through the soul. It is the soul that holds that structure together so that it does not dissolve and flow apart, which we see happen to the bodies of animals when the soul departs. But if this beauty is understood to be in all bodies, the statement forces us to believe that the world itself is also a living being, so that whatever in it imitates constancy is likewise passed on to it from the supreme God through a soul. Plato and very many other philosophers held that this world is a living being, but I have not been able to establish this by sure reasoning, nor have I found that the authority of the divine Scriptures can persuade one of it. I said something that can be taken in this sense in the book On the Immortality of the Soul as well, and I have noted it as rashly said. I do not affirm that it is false that the world is a living being. I only do not grasp that it is true. This, at least, I have no doubt must be held without wavering: this world is not our God, whether it has a soul or not. If it has one, then he who made that soul is our God. If it has none, this world cannot be the god of anything, much less ours. There is, however, a spiritual and living power, even if the world is not a living being, and this power serves God in the holy angels by adorning and governing the world. This is most rightly believed even by those who do not understand it. Here I would use the name "holy angels" for every holy spiritual creature placed in God's secret and hidden ministry. But holy Scripture does not usually call angelic spirits souls. Near the end of this book I said: "The rational and intellectual numbers of blessed and holy souls receive the very law of God, without which not a leaf falls from a tree and by which our hairs are numbered, with no nature coming between, and they pass it on down to earthly and infernal jurisdictions." I do not see how the word "souls" there could be shown to agree with the holy Scriptures. By it I meant only the holy angels, and I do not recall ever having read in the canonical divine oracles that angels have souls.
This book begins thus: "Long enough, almost..."
Chapter 11.
On the Teacher, one book.

During the same period I wrote a book entitled On the Teacher. In it we discuss, inquire and find that the only teacher who teaches a human being knowledge is God. This agrees with what is written in the Gospel: "One is your teacher, Christ."
This book begins thus: "What do you think we wish to accomplish when we speak?"
Chapter 12. On True Religion, one book.

At that time I also wrote a book On True Religion. It argues at great length and in many ways that the one true God, that is, the Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is to be worshipped by true religion. It also shows how great the mercy is by which God has granted human beings the Christian religion, which is the true religion, through his dispensation in time, and how a person is to be drawn gently and fitted for that same worship of God. Above all, however, this book speaks against the two natures of the Manichees.

In one place in this book I said: "Let it be clear and understood by you that there could have been no error in religion if the soul did not worship a soul, or a body, or its own fantasies in place of its God." Here I used "soul" for the whole incorporeal creation, and I was not speaking in the manner of the Scriptures. When the Scriptures do not use the word figuratively, I do not know whether they mean by "soul" anything other than that by which mortal living beings live, and human beings are among these as long as they are mortal. A little later, however, I expressed the same thought better and more briefly when I said: "Let us therefore not serve the creature rather than the Creator, nor become futile in our thoughts, and religion is perfect." By the single word "creature" I meant both kinds, spiritual and bodily. There remains what I said there, "or its own fantasies". This is why I said here, "nor become futile in our thoughts."

I also said: "In our times the Christian religion is the one which it is the safest and surest salvation to know and to follow." This was said with reference to the name, not to the thing itself that bears the name. For the thing now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients as well, and it was never lacking from the beginning of the human race until Christ came in the flesh. From then on the true religion, which already existed, began to be called Christian. After his resurrection and ascension into heaven the apostles began to preach him and very many believed, and then, as it is written, the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. That is why I said, "In our times this is the Christian religion." I did not mean that it did not exist in earlier times, only that it received this name in later times.

In another place I said: "Attend, therefore, to what follows, diligently and devoutly, as far as you can; for God helps such people." This is not to be understood as if he helps only such people. He also helps those who are not such, so that they may become such, that is, so that they may seek diligently and devoutly. But such people he helps so that they may find.

And elsewhere I said: "Then it will follow that after bodily death, which we owe to the first sin, this body will be restored to its original stability in its own time and order." This is to be understood as follows. The original stability of the body, which we lost by sinning, also had such happiness that it did not decline into the weakness of old age. This body will therefore be restored to that original stability in the resurrection of the dead. But it will have more: it will not be sustained by temporal food, but will be given life fully by the spirit alone, when it has risen into a life-giving spirit, since it will then also be spiritual. That first body would not have died if man had not sinned. Even so, it was made a natural body, that is, a living soul.

And elsewhere I said: "Sin is so much a voluntary evil that it is in no way sin if it is not voluntary." This definition may seem false, but careful examination will show it to be entirely true. For we must think here of sin that is only sin, not sin that is also the punishment of sin, as I showed above when I recalled certain passages from the third book On Free Choice. Some sins are not unreasonably called involuntary, because they are committed either in ignorance or under compulsion. Yet even these cannot be committed entirely without the will. Someone who sins in ignorance certainly sins by his will, since he thinks he ought to do what he ought not to do. Again, the flesh lusts against the spirit, and so a person does not do what he wills. He does indeed lust against his will, and in that sense he does not do what he wills. But if he is overcome, he consents to the lust willingly, and in that sense he does only what he wills, being free from righteousness and the slave of sin. Original sin, as it is called in little children, is also not absurdly called voluntary, even though they do not yet use the choice of the will. For it was contracted from the first evil will of man and has become in a sense hereditary. So what I said is not false: "Sin is so much a voluntary evil that it is in no way sin if it is not voluntary." This is why the grace of God does two things. In all who are baptized in Christ it looses the guilt of all past sins, and this is done by the Spirit of regeneration. In adults, the Lord also heals and prepares the will itself, and this is done by the Spirit of faith and love.
In another place I said of the Lord Jesus Christ:

"He did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and admonition." It had not occurred to me that he drove the sellers and buyers out of the temple with a whip. But what does this amount to? He also cast demons out of people against their will, not by persuasive speech but by the force of his power. Again, in another place:

"First," I said, "we must follow those who say that one supreme God alone is to be worshipped; only if the truth does not shine out among them must we move on." This may seem to have been said as if I had doubts about the truth of this religion. But I spoke in a way suited to the person I was writing to. I said, "if the truth does not shine out among them," without the slightest doubt that it would shine out among them. In the same way the apostle says, "If Christ has not risen," without in the least doubting that he has risen.

I also said: "Nor were those miracles allowed to continue into our times, lest the soul should always seek visible things, and the human race grow cold through familiarity with the very things whose novelty had set it on fire." This is indeed true. Nowadays, when hands are laid on the baptized, they do not receive the Holy Spirit in such a way that they speak in the tongues of all nations. Nor are the sick healed now by the passing shadow of Christ's preachers. And if any other such things were done then, they clearly ceased later. But what I said is not to be taken to mean that we should believe no miracles are done now in the name of Christ. When I wrote that very book, I already knew that a blind man had been given his sight at the bodies of the martyrs of Milan, in that same city. I knew of several other such things as well. So many happen even in these times that we can neither know them all nor count up the ones we do know.

In another place I said, "As the apostle says, 'All order is from God.'" The apostle did not say this in these words, although the meaning seems to be the same. What he said was: "The things that are, are ordained by God."

And elsewhere I said: "Let no one deceive us at all: whatever is rightly blamed is rejected by comparison with something better." This was said of substances and natures, which were the subject under discussion. It was not said of good actions and sins.

And also elsewhere I said: "But not even so should one human being love another in the way that brothers according to the flesh are loved, or sons, or spouses, or any kinsmen, relations by marriage or fellow citizens; for this love too is temporal. We would have no such ties, which arise through birth and death, if our nature had remained in God's commandments and image and had not been banished into this corruption." I wholly reject this thought, as I have already rejected it above in connection with the first book On Genesis against the Manichees. For it leads to the belief that the first married couple would not have had human offspring if they had not sinned, as though their children would necessarily have been mortal if they were born from the union of male and female. I had not yet seen that immortal children could have been born of immortal parents if that great sin had not changed human nature for the worse. In that case fruitfulness and happiness would have remained in both parents and children. Human beings would have been born up to the fixed number of the saints that God predestined, not to succeed parents who died but to reign with parents who lived. So these kinships and ties of marriage would exist even if no one sinned and no one died.

In another place I said: "Let us tend toward the one God, binding our souls to him alone, from which binding religion is believed to take its name (religantes, religio), and let us be free of all superstition." The account I gave in these words of how religio got its name is the one I preferred. For I am well aware that Latin authors have proposed another origin for the word: that religio is so called because it is "chosen again" (religitur). This verb is compounded from legere, that is, eligere (to choose), so that in Latin religo would seem to be formed like eligo.
This book begins thus: "Since the way of every good and happy life..."
Chapter 13. On the Usefulness of Belief, one book.

Then, as a priest at Hippo Regius, I wrote a book On the Usefulness of Belief to a friend of mine. I knew that he had been deceived by the Manichees and was still held in that error. He mocked the discipline of the Catholic faith because people were ordered to believe instead of being taught by most certain reasoning what was true.

In this book I said: "Yet in those precepts and commandments of the Law which Christians may not now observe, such as the sabbath, circumcision, sacrifices and anything else of this kind, such great mysteries are contained that every devout person understands this: nothing is more harmful than taking anything there according to the letter, that is, word for word, and nothing is more wholesome than having it revealed by the spirit. Hence: 'The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.'" But I explained these words of the apostle Paul differently in the book entitled On the Spirit and the Letter. That explanation is, it seems to me, much more fitting, or rather the matter itself shows it to be so, although the sense given here is not to be rejected either.

I also said: "There are two kinds of people who are praiseworthy in religion. The first are those who have already found, and they must also be judged most blessed. The second are those who search most zealously and most rightly. The first are already in possession; the others are on the way, by which, however, one arrives most surely." Those who have already found, whom I said were already in possession, may be taken to be most blessed not in this life but in the life we hope for and travel toward by the way of faith. If my words are understood in that sense, they contain no error. For those who are already where we desire to arrive by seeking and believing, that is, by keeping to the way of faith, must be judged to have found what was to be sought. But if such people are thought to exist, or to have existed, in this life, that does not seem true to me. It is not that nothing true at all can be found in this life that the mind discerns rather than faith believes. It is that whatever is found here, however great, does not make anyone most blessed. The apostle says, "We see now through a mirror, in an enigma," and "Now I know in part." This does not mean that what is known in part is not discerned by the mind. It is plainly discerned, but it does not yet make us most blessed. What makes us most blessed is what he goes on to say: "but then face to face," and "then I shall know, even as I am known." Those who have found this must be said to be established in the possession of blessedness. The way of faith that we hold leads there, and we desire to arrive there by believing. But who those most blessed ones are, who are already in the possession to which this way leads, is a great question. That the holy angels are there is no question at all. But it is rightly asked whether holy people who have already died should be said to be established in that possession already. They have indeed been stripped of the corruptible body that weighs down the soul. Yet they too are still awaiting the redemption of their body, and their flesh rests in hope and does not yet shine in the incorruption to come. Whether they lack anything on this account in contemplating the truth with the eyes of the heart, "face to face," as it is said, this is not the place to inquire.

I also said: "For to know great and honorable, or even divine, things is most blessed." We should refer this to that same blessedness. In this life, however much of such things is known, it is not yet most blessed, because what remains unknown of them is incomparably greater.

I also said that "it makes a great difference whether something is held by the sure reasoning of the mind, which we call knowing, or is usefully handed on to later generations by report or writings to be believed." A little later I said, "What we know, therefore, we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority." This is not to be taken to mean that in more ordinary speech we should be afraid to say we know what we believe on the word of reliable witnesses. Strictly speaking, of course, we say we know only what we grasp by the firm reasoning of the mind. But when we use words better suited to common usage, as divine Scripture also does, we should not hesitate to say that we know both what we perceive with our bodily senses and what we believe on the word of trustworthy witnesses, provided we understand how these differ from knowledge in the strict sense.

I also said: "No one doubts that all people are either foolish or wise." This may seem to contradict what we read in the third book On Free Choice: "as if human nature admitted no intermediate state besides foolish and wise." But that was said where the question concerned the first man: was he made wise, or foolish, or neither? We could not possibly call him foolish, since he was made without fault and folly is a great fault. Yet it was not clear enough how we could call him wise, since he could be led astray. So, to put it briefly, I chose to say: "as if human nature admitted no intermediate state besides folly and wisdom." I was also thinking of little children. We confess that they contract original sin, yet we cannot properly call them either wise or foolish, since they are not yet using free choice either well or badly. Here, however, when I said that all people are either wise or foolish, I meant those who already use reason, which sets them apart from beasts and makes them human. In the same way we say that all people want to be happy. When we make a statement so true and so evident, surely we are not afraid that it will be taken to include little children, who are not yet able to want this?

In another place I mentioned the miracles the Lord Jesus did when he was here in the flesh, and then added: "Why, you will say, do these things not happen now?" I replied: "Because they would not move people unless they were marvelous, and if they were usual, they would not be marvelous." I said this because miracles as great as those, and as many, do not happen now. I did not mean that none happen even now.

At the end of the book I said: "But since this discussion of ours has gone on much longer than I expected, let us end the book here. I want you to remember that in it I have not yet begun to refute the Manichees or to attack their nonsense. Nor have I disclosed anything great about the Catholic Church itself. I only wished to root out of you, if I could, the false opinion about true Christians that has been spread against us out of malice or ignorance, and to rouse you to learn certain great and divine things. So let this volume stand as it is. When your mind has become calmer, I shall perhaps be readier with the rest." I did not say this as if I had written nothing against the Manichees so far, or had put nothing about Catholic doctrine into writing. The many volumes I had already published bear witness that I had not been silent on either subject. But in this book, written to him, I had not yet begun to refute the Manichees or to attack their nonsense, nor had I disclosed anything great about the Catholic Church itself. For I hoped that, once this beginning was made, I would write to him what I had not written here.
This book begins thus: "If, Honoratus, it seemed to me that one and the same thing..."
Chapter 14. On the Two Souls, one book.

After this book, while still a presbyter, I wrote against the Manichees On the Two Souls. They say that one of these souls is part of God, and the other comes from the race of darkness, which God did not create and which is coeternal with God. They rave that both these souls, one good and the other evil, are present in a single human being. The evil one, they say, belongs properly to the flesh, and the flesh, they also say, is of the race of darkness. The good one comes from a part of God that arrived from outside and fought with the race of darkness, and the two are mixed together. So they attribute everything good in a human being to that good soul, and everything evil to that evil soul.

In this book I said that there is no life of any kind which, by the very fact that it is life and to the extent that it is life at all, does not belong to the supreme fount and source of life. I meant this to be understood as a creature belonging to its Creator, not to suggest that it comes from him as a part of him.

Again, I said that sin is "nowhere, that is, except in the will." The Pelagians may think this was said in their favor because of little children. They deny that infants have original sin to be forgiven them in baptism, because they do not yet exercise the choice of the will. As if the sin which we say they contract from Adam by origin, that is, by being bound up in his guilt and held liable to punishment because of it, could ever have existed except from the will! It was by the will that this sin was committed, when the divine command was transgressed. One might also think the statement false in which we said that sin is nowhere except in the will, because the apostle said: "But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me." This sin is so far from being in the will that he says: "What I do not want, that I do." How then is sin nowhere except in the will? But the sin of which the apostle spoke in this way is called sin because it was brought about by sin and is the punishment of sin. For this is said of the concupiscence of the flesh, as he makes clear in what follows: "I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh; for to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not." The accomplishment of the good is that not even the concupiscence of sin should remain in a person. When someone lives well, the will does not consent to that concupiscence; yet he does not accomplish the good, because it is still present in the concupiscence which the will resists. The guilt of this concupiscence is dissolved in baptism, but the weakness remains, and every believer who is making good progress struggles against it with the greatest zeal until it is healed. But the sin which is nowhere except in the will is to be understood above all as the sin which just condemnation followed, for it was this that "entered the world through one man"; although the sin by which one consents to the concupiscence of sin is also committed only by the will. For this reason I said in another place as well: "Therefore there is no sinning except by the will."

Likewise in another place I defined the will itself, saying: "The will is a movement of the mind, under no compulsion, either toward not losing something or toward obtaining something." This was said so that this definition might distinguish one who is willing from one who is unwilling, and so that attention might thus be directed to those who were first in paradise and became the origin of evil for the human race by sinning under no compulsion, that is, by sinning with free will. For they acted against the command knowingly, and the tempter persuaded them to do it; he did not compel them. Indeed, someone who sinned unknowingly may not inappropriately be said to have sinned unwillingly. Yet what he did unknowingly he still did willingly, and so even his sin could not exist without the will. That will was certainly, as it was defined, a movement of the soul, under no compulsion, either toward not losing something or toward obtaining something. For what he would not have done had he not wanted to, he was not compelled to do. He did it, then, because he wanted to, even though he did not sin because he wanted to, since he did not know that what he did was a sin. So even such a sin could not exist without the will; but it was a will to the deed, not a will to the sin, and yet the deed was a sin, for what was done ought not to have been done. Someone who sins knowingly, if he is able to resist what pushes him toward sin without sinning and yet does not do so, certainly sins willingly, since whoever is able to resist is not compelled to give way. But someone who cannot resist with his will the desire that compels him, and therefore acts against the precepts of justice, commits a sin of such a kind that it is also the punishment of sin. Therefore it is entirely true that sin cannot exist without the will.

Likewise the definition of sin in which we said, "Sin is the will to retain or to obtain what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain," is true because what is defined there is that which is only sin, not that which is also the punishment of sin. For when sin is of such a kind that it is at the same time the punishment of sin, how much can the will do under the dominion of desire, unless perhaps, if it is devout, pray for help? It is free to the extent that it has been set free, and to that extent it is called will. Otherwise it should properly be called desire rather than will. This desire is not, as the Manichees foolishly suppose, something added from an alien nature, but a fault of our own nature, from which it is healed only by the grace of the Savior. If anyone says that even this desire is nothing other than the will, but a vicious will that serves sin, there is no need to oppose him or to quarrel about words when the reality is agreed upon. For in this way too it is shown that there is no sin without the will, whether in act or in origin.

Again, I said: "I had already begun to ask whether that evil race of souls, before it was mixed with the good, had any will. For if it had none, it will be without sin and innocent, and therefore in no way evil." "Why then," they say, "do you speak of the sin of little children, whose will you do not hold guilty?" The answer is that they are held guilty not through any will of their own, but through their origin. For what is every earthly human being by origin but Adam? And Adam certainly had a will, and when he sinned by that will, sin entered the world through him.

Likewise, where I said, "Souls can in no way be evil by nature," if someone asks how we are to understand what the apostle says, "We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest," we answer that in these words of mine I meant the nature that is properly called nature, in which we were created without fault. For the nature the apostle speaks of is called nature because of our origin, and that origin certainly has a fault, which is contrary to nature.

And again, it was said: "To hold anyone guilty of sin because he did not do what he was unable to do is the height of injustice and madness." "Why then," they say, "are little children held guilty?" The answer is that they are held guilty by their origin from one who did not do what he was able to do, namely, keep the divine command.
