I also said: "Whatever those souls do, if they do it by nature and not by will, that is, if they lack a free movement of the mind both toward doing and toward not doing, if in short they are granted no power to abstain from their own work, we cannot hold that sin is theirs." The question about little children does not trouble this statement, because they are held guilty by their origin from one who sinned by his will, when he did not lack a free movement of the mind both toward doing and toward not doing, and had full power to abstain from the evil work. The Manichees say no such thing about the race of darkness, which they bring in with the most fabulous inventions, and they contend that its nature was always evil and never good.

One may ask how I could have said: "Even if there are souls (which for the moment is uncertain) devoted to bodily functions not by sin but by nature, and which touch us by a certain inner closeness, although they are inferior, they should not be held evil on that account, because it is we who are evil when we follow them and love bodily things." I said this about the souls of which I had begun to speak more openly when I said: "Even if it were granted to them that we are enticed to shameful things by another, inferior kind of souls, they do not thereby prove either that those natures are evil or that these are the supreme good." For I carried the discussion of these souls up to the passage where I said: "Even if there are souls (which for the moment is uncertain) devoted to bodily functions not by sin but by nature," and so on. So it may be asked why I said, "which for the moment is uncertain," when I ought not to have doubted at all that there are no such souls. But I said this because I had met people who said that the devil and his angels are good in their own kind and in the nature in which God created them, such as they are, in their proper order; but that it is evil for us if we are enticed and led astray by them, and honorable and glorious if we guard against them and overcome them. Those who say this think they can bring suitable testimonies from the scriptures to prove it, such as what is written in the book of Job where the devil is described: "This is the beginning of the Lord's creation, which he made to be mocked by his angels"; or the verse in Psalm 103: "This dragon, which you formed to mock him." This question would have had to be taken up and resolved not against the Manichees, who do not hold this view, but against others who do. I did not want to treat and unravel it then, lest I make the book much longer than I wished, since I saw that even if this were granted, the Manichees should and could still be refuted for introducing, in their most insane error, a nature of evil coeternal with the eternal good. That is why I said, "which for the moment is uncertain": not because I had any doubt about it, but because the question had not yet been settled between me and those whom I had found to hold this opinion. I did, however, settle it with as much clarity as I could, according to the holy scriptures, in other books of mine written much later, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis.

In another place I said: "We sin by loving bodily things, because we are both commanded by justice and able by nature to love spiritual things, and then we are at our best and happy in our own kind." Here it may be asked why I said "able by nature" and not "by grace." But the question being argued against the Manichees concerned nature; and grace certainly brings it about that this nature, which in its corrupted state is unable, becomes able through him who "came to seek and to save what was lost." Yet even then I was mindful of this grace, and I prayed for my closest friends who were still held by that deadly error, saying: "Great God, almighty God, God of supreme goodness, whom it is right to believe and to understand as inviolable and incorruptible, threefold unity whom the Catholic Church worships, I humbly pray, having experienced your mercy in myself: do not allow those men with whom I have been in the fullest agreement in human life since boyhood to disagree with me in your worship." Praying in this way, I already held by faith not only that those who have turned to God are helped by his grace to make progress and be made perfect (and here it could still be said that this grace is given as a reward for their conversion), but also that their very turning to God belongs to the grace of God. I prayed to him for those who had turned far away from him, and I prayed that they might turn to him.
This book begins thus: "With the help of God's mercy."
CHAPTER 15
PROCEEDINGS AGAINST FORTUNATUS THE MANICHEE, ONE BOOK

At the same time, during my presbyterate, I held a debate against a certain Fortunatus, a presbyter of the Manichees, who had lived a long time at Hippo and had led so many astray that he enjoyed living there because of them. Our debate was taken down by stenographers as we argued, as if official records were being made, for it bears both the date and the consul. I took care to have it put into a book to be preserved. The question treated there is the origin of evil. I maintained that human evil arose from the free choice of the will, while he tried to argue for a nature of evil coeternal with God. But on the following day he finally admitted that he could find nothing to say against us. He did not in fact become a Catholic, but he did leave Hippo.

In this book I said: "I say that the soul was made by God, like all the other things that were made by God, and that among the things God almighty made, the chief place was given to the soul." I meant this to be taken generally of the whole rational creation, although it is either not at all or not easily found in the holy scriptures that angels are said to have souls, as we have already said above.

Likewise in another place I said: "I say that there is no sin if one does not sin by one's own will." There I meant that sin to be understood which is not also the punishment of sin; for about that kind of punishment I said what needed to be said elsewhere in the same debate.

I also said: "so that afterward the very flesh which tormented us with punishments while we remained in sin may be made subject to us in the resurrection, and may not shake us with any adversity to keep us from observing the law and the divine commands." This is not to be understood as though in that kingdom of God, where we shall have an incorruptible and immortal body, the law and commands are still to be taken from the divine scriptures. Rather, the eternal law will be kept there most perfectly, and we shall hold those two commands about loving God and neighbor not by reading them, but in perfect and everlasting love itself.
This work begins thus: "On the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Arcadius Augustus, for the second time, and Rufinus, men of senatorial rank."
CHAPTER 16
ON FAITH AND THE CREED, ONE BOOK

Around the same time, at the command of the bishops who were holding a plenary council of all Africa at Hippo Regius, I gave a discourse in their presence on faith and the creed. At the very earnest urging of some of them who were especially fond of me, I put that discourse into a book. In it the matters themselves are discussed, but without the exact form of words that is handed over to candidates for baptism to be learned by heart.

In this book, when the resurrection of the flesh was being treated, I said: "The body will rise, according to the Christian faith, which cannot be deceived. Whoever finds this incredible pays attention to what the flesh is like now, but does not consider what it will be like, because at that time of angelic transformation it will no longer be flesh and blood, but only body," and the rest of what I discussed there about the change of earthly bodies into heavenly bodies, since the apostle, speaking of this, said: "Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God." But anyone who takes these words to mean that the earthly body we now have will be changed into a heavenly body at the resurrection in such a way that neither these members nor the substance of flesh will remain should certainly be corrected and reminded of the Lord's body. After the resurrection he appeared in the same members, not only to be seen with the eyes but also to be handled with the hands, and he also confirmed in words that he had flesh, saying: "Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." It is clear from this that the apostle did not deny that the substance of flesh will be in the kingdom of God. Rather, by the name "flesh and blood" he meant either those who live according to the flesh, or the corruption of the flesh itself, which will certainly not exist then. For after he had said, "Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God," he immediately added, as if explaining what he meant, and so it is rightly understood: "nor will corruption possess incorruption." Anyone who reads the last book of The City of God will find that I have discussed this matter, which is hard to persuade unbelievers of, as carefully as I could.
This book begins thus: "Since it is written."
CHAPTER 17
ON THE LITERAL MEANING OF GENESIS, ONE UNFINISHED BOOK

I had written two books on Genesis against the Manichees. Because in them I had treated the words of scripture according to their allegorical meaning, not daring to expound such great secrets of the natural world literally, that is, to show how what is said there could be taken in its proper historical sense, I wanted to test what I could do in this most laborious and difficult task as well. But in expounding the scriptures my inexperience collapsed under the weight of so great a load, and before I had finished even one book I gave up a labor I could not sustain. But in this present work, while I was reviewing my writings, this very book came into my hands, unfinished as it was. I had not published it and had decided to destroy it, since I later wrote twelve books entitled On the Literal Meaning of Genesis. Although in those books more questions seem to have been raised than answers found, this one is in no way to be compared with them. Yet after reviewing this one too, I decided to let it stand, so that it might serve as an indication, not a useless one, I think, of my first attempts at explaining and investigating the divine words; and I wished its title to be On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, Unfinished. I found that it had been dictated up to these words: "Yet the Father is the Father, and the Son is nothing other than the Son; for even when he is called the likeness of the Father, although this shows that no unlikeness comes between them, still the Father is not alone if he has a likeness." After this I had repeated the words of scripture to be considered and treated again: "And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness." I had left the book unfinished at the point dictated up to there. What follows in it I thought should be added when I reviewed it; but even so I did not finish it, and left it unfinished even with this addition. For if I had finished it, I would at least have discussed all the works and words of God that belong to the sixth day. It seemed superfluous to me to point out in this book the same things that displease me, or to defend things that might displease others because they are not well understood. Instead I briefly advise that those twelve books, which I wrote much later, be read, and that this one be judged by them.
This one, then, begins thus: "Obscure questions about natural things, which we perceive to have been made by God the almighty Craftsman, are to be treated by inquiring, not by asserting."
CHAPTER 18
ON THE LORD'S SERMON ON THE MOUNT, TWO BOOKS
Around the same time I wrote two volumes on the Lord's Sermon on the Mount according to Matthew.

In the first of these books, on account of what is written, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God,” I said: “Wisdom befits the peacemakers, in whom all things are now set in order and no impulse rebels against reason, but everything obeys the spirit of man, since that spirit itself obeys God.” It is fair to ask how I could have said this. For no one in this life can reach the point where the law that wars against the law of the mind is entirely absent from his members. Even if a man's spirit resisted it so firmly that he never slipped into consenting to it, it would still fight against him. So the statement that no impulse rebels against reason can rightly be understood of peacemakers who are now at work taming the desires of the flesh, so that they may one day arrive at that fullest peace.

In another place, after repeating the same saying from the Gospel, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God,” I added: “And these things can indeed be fulfilled in this life, as we believe they were fulfilled in the apostles.” This must be understood in the right way. It does not mean that we suppose no impulse of the flesh fought against the spirit in the apostles while they lived here. It means that these things can be fulfilled here to the extent that we believe they were fulfilled in the apostles, that is, in the measure of human perfection that is possible in this life. For I did not say, “These things can be fulfilled in this life, for we believe they were fulfilled in the apostles.” What I said was, “as we believe they were fulfilled in the apostles,” meaning that they are fulfilled in the way they were fulfilled in them, that is, with the kind of perfection this life can hold. They are not fulfilled in the way they are to be fulfilled in that fullest peace for which we hope, when it will be said: “Where, O death, is your struggle?”

In another place I cited the text, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure,” but I had not yet understood that it applies more truly and properly to Christ. For if the Spirit were not given to other men by measure, Elisha would not have asked for double what there was in Elijah.

Again, when I was explaining the text, “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things are accomplished,” I said that it could mean nothing other than a forceful expression of perfection. Here it is fair to ask whether this perfection can be understood in a way that still leaves it true that no one who has the use of free will lives here without sin. For who can fulfill the law down to a single stroke, except the one who carries out all the divine commandments? But among those very commandments is the one that tells us to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” a prayer that the whole Church says until the end of the age. So all the commandments are counted as done when whatever is not done is forgiven.

As for what the Lord says, “Whoever, then, relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others so,” and so on, down to the place where he says, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” I explained this much better and more fittingly in other, later sermons of mine, and it would take too long to go over it again here. The sense there comes down to this: the righteousness of those who both say and do is greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees. For in another place the Lord himself says of the scribes and Pharisees, “For they say, and do not do.” Later we also understood better what is written:

“Whoever is angry with his brother.” For the Greek manuscripts do not have “without cause,” as it is given here, although the sense is the same. We said that one must consider what it means to be angry with one's brother, since a man who is angry at his brother's sin is not angry with his brother. So whoever is angry with his brother rather than with his sin is angry without cause.

Again, I said: “This is to be understood of father and mother and the other ties of blood, so that in them we hate what has fallen to the human race through being born and dying.” This sounds as though these relationships would not have existed if no one died, had no sin of human nature come first. I have already rejected that view above. For there would certainly have been kinship and marriage ties even if the human race had grown and multiplied without death and without any original sin. So the question why the Lord commanded us to love our enemies, when in another place he commands us to hate even parents and children, must be resolved differently, not as it was resolved here but as we have often resolved it since: namely, that we should love our enemies so as to win them for the kingdom of God, and should hate in our relatives whatever hinders us from the kingdom of God.

Again, concerning the commandment that forbids a man to divorce his wife except for fornication, I discussed it here very scrupulously. But what kind of fornication the Lord means, for which it is lawful to divorce a wife, must be thought over and examined again and again. Is it the fornication that is condemned in sexual misconduct, or the kind of which it is said, “You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you”? The latter certainly includes the former, for anyone who takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a prostitute does commit fornication away from the Lord. In a matter so great and so hard to sort out, I do not want the reader to think that this discussion of ours should be enough for him. Let him also read what has been written later, whether by us or by others who have considered and treated it better. Or let him, if he can, examine with a more watchful and intelligent mind the points here that may rightly trouble him. It is not that every sin is fornication, for God does not destroy everyone who sins, since he daily hears his saints saying, “Forgive us our debts,” whereas he does destroy everyone who commits fornication away from him. But how far this fornication is to be understood and where its limits lie, and whether it is lawful to divorce a wife on account of it, is a very obscure question. That it is lawful on account of the fornication committed in sexual misconduct, however, is no question at all. And where I said that this is permitted, not commanded, I did not pay attention to another passage of Scripture which says, “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and ungodly.” Yet I would certainly not say that the woman should still have been considered an adulteress after she heard from the Lord, “Neither will I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more,” if she heard this and obeyed.

In another place I defined the sin of a brother that leads to death, of which the apostle John says, “I do not say that one should pray for that,” in these words: “I think the sin of a brother that leads to death is when someone, after coming to know God through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, attacks the brotherhood and is driven by the firebrands of envy against the very grace by which he was reconciled to God.” I did not state this firmly, since I said that I thought so. Still, I ought to have added: “if he ends this life in such wicked perversity of mind.” For we must never despair of anyone, however wicked, while he is still in this life, and it is not out of place to pray for someone of whom we do not despair.

Likewise in the second book I said: “No one will be allowed to be ignorant of the kingdom of God when his Only-begotten comes from heaven, not only in a way the mind can grasp but also visibly, in the Lord's man, to judge the living and the dead.” But I do not see that he who is the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, is rightly called “the Lord's man” [since he is in fact the Lord]. For who in his holy household cannot be called a man of the Lord? I said this, indeed, because I had read it in certain Catholic commentators on the divine Scriptures. But wherever I said it, I wish I had not. For I saw later that it should not be said, although it can be defended on some grounds.
Again, I said: “For hardly anyone's conscience can hate God.” I do not think this should have been said. For there are many of whom it is said: “the pride of those who hate you.”

In another place I said: “The Lord said, ‘Each day's trouble is enough for it,’ because necessity itself compelled people to take food. I think this is called ‘trouble’ because it is a punishment for us, for it belongs to the frailty we have deserved by sinning.” In saying this I did not take into account that bodily nourishment was also given to the first human beings in paradise, before they deserved this penalty of death by sinning. For they were immortal in a body that was not yet spiritual but natural, in such a way that even with this kind of immortality they made use of bodily food.

Again, when I said, “the glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle, which God chose for himself,” I did not say it because the Church is already like this in every respect now, although there is no doubt that it was chosen in order to be like this when Christ, its life, appears. For then it too will appear with him in glory, and it is on account of this glory that it is called the glorious Church.

Again, on what the Lord says, “Ask and you will receive, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened to you,” I thought I should explain, at some length, how these three differ from one another. But it is far better to refer them all to asking with the greatest persistence. He shows this himself when he sums them all up in a single word, saying, “How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” For he did not say, “to those who ask, seek, and knock.”
This work begins thus: “The sermon which the Lord spoke.”
CHAPTER 19.
PSALM AGAINST THE PARTY OF DONATUS, ONE BOOK.

Wishing also to bring the case of the Donatists to the knowledge of the humblest common people, the wholly uneducated and unlearned, and to fix it in their memory as far as we could, I composed a psalm for them to sing, following the order of the Latin alphabet, but only as far as the letter V. Psalms of this kind are called abecedarian. I left out the last three letters, and in their place I added a final section as a kind of epilogue, in which Mother Church addresses them. The refrain that is sung in response, and the prologue setting out the case, which we also wanted to be sung, are not in alphabetical order; the alphabetical order begins after the prologue. I did not want to write it in any kind of meter, so that the demands of meter would not force me to use words less familiar to ordinary people.
This psalm begins thus: “All you who rejoice in peace, now judge what is true,” which is its refrain.
CHAPTER 20. AGAINST THE LETTER OF DONATUS THE HERETIC, ONE BOOK.

In the same period of my priesthood I also wrote a book against the letter of Donatus, who was the second bishop of the party of Donatus at Carthage, after Majorinus. In that letter he argues that Christ's baptism should be believed to exist only within his communion. We contradict him in this book.

In it I said in one place of the apostle Peter that the Church was founded on him as on a rock. This sense is also sung by many in the verses of the most blessed Ambrose, where he says of the cockerel: “At its crowing, the very rock of the Church washed away his guilt.” But I know that I have since very often explained the Lord's words, “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church,” to mean that the rock is the one whom Peter confessed when he said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Peter, then, named after this rock, represented the person of the Church, which is built on this rock and has received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For he was not told, “You are the rock,” but “You are Peter.” The rock was Christ, and because Simon confessed him, as the whole Church confesses him, he was called Peter. Let the reader choose which of these two interpretations is the more probable.

In another place I said: “God seeks no one's death.” This should be understood to mean that man brought death on himself by abandoning God, and brings it on himself still if he does not return to God, as it is written: “God did not make death.” Yet this is no less true: “Life and death are from the Lord God,” life from him as giver, death from him as avenger.

Again, I said that Donatus, whose letter I was refuting, had asked the emperor to appoint bishops from overseas to judge between him and Caecilian. It turns out to be more probable that it was not he who did this but another Donatus, of the same schism. That Donatus was not the Donatist bishop of Carthage but the bishop of Casae Nigrae, though he was the first to commit that wicked schism at Carthage.

Nor indeed did Donatus of Carthage establish the practice of rebaptizing Christians, as I had believed he did when I was answering his letter. Nor did he himself remove words essential to the meaning from the middle of a sentence in the book of Wisdom. Where it is written, “If someone is washed after touching a corpse and touches it again, what does his washing gain him?” he quoted it as though it read, “If someone is washed after touching a corpse, what does his washing gain him?” We later learned that even before the party of Donatus existed, a great many manuscripts, though African ones, read it this way, without “and touches it again” in the middle. Had I known this then, I would not have said such harsh things against him as a thief or violator of the divine word.
This book begins thus: “I had heard from you yourself, when you were present.”
CHAPTER 21.
AGAINST ADIMANTUS, A DISCIPLE OF MANI, ONE BOOK.

At the same time certain disputations of Adimantus, who had been a disciple of Mani, came into my hands. He wrote them against the Law and the Prophets, trying to show that the writings of the Gospels and the apostles contradicted them. I answered him by setting out his words and giving my reply to them. I put all this into one volume, and in it I answered certain questions not once but twice, because my first reply had been lost and was found only after I had already answered a second time. Some of these same questions I dealt with in sermons preached to the people in church. Some I have still not answered; others remained, passed over because more pressing matters came up, and then forgotten as well.

In this book I said: “Before the Lord's coming, the people who received the Old Testament were held under certain shadows and figures of things, according to a wonderful and well-ordered arrangement of the ages. Yet in it there is so much proclamation and foretelling of the New Testament that no precepts or promises are found in the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, however lofty and divine, that are lacking in those old books as well.” But I should have added “almost” and said: “so that almost no precepts or promises are found in the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, however lofty and divine, that are lacking in those old books as well.” For what would be the point of the Lord saying in his sermon on the mount, “You have heard that this was said to the people of old, but I say to you this,” if he himself commanded nothing more than was commanded in those old books? Moreover, we do not read that the kingdom of heaven was promised to that people among the promises of the law given through Moses on Mount Sinai, which is properly called the Old Testament, and which the apostle says was prefigured by Sarah's slave woman and her son. Yet the New Testament too was prefigured there, by Sarah herself and her son. So if the figures are examined, everything is found prophesied there that has been brought to pass through Christ, or that is awaited to be brought to pass through him. Nevertheless, because of certain precepts that are not figurative but literal, which are found not in the Old but in the New, it would be said more cautiously and modestly that almost nothing is here that is not also there, rather than nothing, even though there are found there those two commandments about the love of God and of neighbor, to which everything in the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the apostles is most rightly referred.

Again, I said: “The name ‘sons’ is used in the Scriptures in three ways.” This was said without enough thought. For we undoubtedly left out certain other ways, as when someone is called a son of Gehenna or an adopted son, which are not said by nature, nor by teaching, nor by imitation. We gave examples of these three ways as though they were the only ones: by nature, as the Jews are sons of Abraham; by teaching, as the apostle calls those he taught the gospel his sons; by imitation, as we are sons of Abraham, whose faith we imitate.

When I said, “When it has put on incorruption and immortality, it will no longer be flesh and blood,” I said that it would no longer be flesh in the sense of fleshly corruption, not in the sense of substance; in that sense even the Lord's body after the resurrection was called flesh.

In another place I said: “Unless someone changes his will, he cannot do good.” In another passage the Lord teaches that this lies within our power, where he says: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad.” This is not contrary to the grace of God that we preach. It is indeed within a man's power to change his will for the better; but that power is nothing unless it is given by God, of whom it is said: “He gave them power to become children of God.” For since what is in our power is what we do when we will to do it, nothing is so much in our power as the will itself. But the will is prepared by the Lord. That, then, is how he gives the power.

This is also how to understand what I said later: “It is in our power to deserve either to be grafted in by God's goodness or to be cut off by his severity.” For nothing is in our power except what we attain by our will. When the Lord prepares that will to be strong and powerful, the work of devotion becomes easy, even what was once difficult and impossible.
This book begins thus: “Concerning what is written: In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”
CHAPTER 22.
EXPOSITION OF CERTAIN PROPOSITIONS FROM THE APOSTLE'S LETTER TO THE ROMANS.

While I was still a priest, it happened that at Carthage the apostle's letter to the Romans was being read among those of us who were together there. Some of the brothers asked me certain questions, and when I answered as well as I could, they wanted what I said to be written down rather than poured out without any record. When I did as they asked, one more book was added to my earlier works.

In that book I said: "The statement 'We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal' shows clearly enough that the law cannot be fulfilled except by spiritual people, such as the grace of God makes them." I certainly did not mean this to be taken as spoken in the person of the apostle, who was already spiritual, but in the person of a man placed under the law and not yet under grace. That is how I formerly understood these words. Afterwards I read certain commentators on the divine scriptures whose authority carried weight with me. I then considered the matter more carefully and saw that the words "We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal" can also be understood of the apostle himself. I have shown this as carefully as I could in the books I recently wrote against the Pelagians. In this book, then, I said that the words "But I am carnal," and the rest up to the place where he says, "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord," describe a man still under the law and not yet established under grace. Such a man wants to do good, but he is overcome by the concupiscence of the flesh and does evil. From the dominion of this concupiscence nothing frees him except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, by the gift of the Holy Spirit. Through the Spirit, love is poured out in our hearts and conquers the concupiscences of the flesh, so that we do not consent to them and do evil but rather do good. By this the Pelagian heresy is in fact already overthrown, for it holds that the love by which we live good and godly lives comes not from God but from ourselves. But in the books we have published against the Pelagians we have shown that these words are better understood as also being those of a spiritual man who is already established under grace. This is because of the body of flesh, which is not yet spiritual but will be in the resurrection of the dead. It is also because of the concupiscence of the flesh itself. The saints struggle against it and do not consent to it for evil, yet in this life they are not free of the impulses they resist and fight against. They will not have them in that other life, however, where death will be swallowed up in victory. Because of this concupiscence and its impulses, which are resisted but are still present in us, any saint already placed under grace can say all the things that I said were the words of a man not yet under grace but under the law. To show this here would take too long, and I have already stated where I have shown it.

Again, I discussed what God chose in the one not yet born, of whom he said that the elder would serve him, and what he rejected in that elder one, who was likewise not yet born. The prophetic testimony "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" is cited concerning them for this reason, though it was uttered long afterward. In that discussion I carried the reasoning to the point of saying: "God therefore did not choose anyone's works in foreknowledge, since he himself is going to give them. But he chose faith in foreknowledge. The one he foreknew would believe in him is the one he chose, to give him the Holy Spirit, so that by doing good works he might also attain eternal life." When I said this, I had not yet inquired more carefully into the election of grace, nor had I yet discovered what it is. The same apostle says of it: "A remnant has come about through the election of grace." This is certainly not grace if any merits come before it. Otherwise what is given would no longer be given according to grace but paid according to what is owed, rendered to merits rather than bestowed as a gift. Accordingly, consider what I said immediately afterwards:

"For the same apostle says, 'It is the same God who works all things in all'; but nowhere is it said, 'God believes all things in all.'" And then I added: "So our believing is our own, but our doing good belongs to him who gives the Spirit to those who believe." I certainly ought not to have said this if I had already known that faith itself is also found among the gifts of God that are given in the same Spirit. Both, then, are ours because of the choice of the will, and yet both are given because of the Spirit of faith and love. For it is not love alone, but, as it is written, "love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ."

A little later I said: "For it is ours to believe and to will, but his to give to those who believe and will the ability to do good through the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured out in our hearts." This is indeed true, but by the same rule both belong to him, because he prepares the will, and both belong to us, because they do not happen unless we will them.

For this reason, consider what I also said later: "For we cannot even will unless we are called. And when we have willed after the calling, our will and our running are not enough unless God both gives strength to those who run and brings them to where he calls." Then I added: "It is clear, therefore, that our doing good is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy." This is entirely true. But I said too little about the calling itself that takes place according to God's purpose. For not all who are called are called in this way, but only the elect.

A little later I said: "For just as in those whom God has chosen, [not works but] faith begins merit, so that they do good by God's gift, so in those whom he condemns, unbelief and impiety begin the merit of punishment, so that through that very punishment they also do evil." What I said was entirely true. But I neither thought it necessary to inquire whether the merit of faith is itself also a gift of God, nor did I say so.

And in another place I said: "For the one on whom he has mercy he makes to do good, and the one whom he hardens he abandons, so that he does evil. But that mercy is granted to the preceding merit of faith, and this hardening to preceding impiety." This is indeed true, but it still remained to ask whether the merit of faith also comes from God's mercy. That is, it remained to ask whether this mercy is shown to a person only because he is a believer, or whether it was also shown so that he might become a believer. For we read the apostle saying, "I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful." He does not say, "because I was faithful." So mercy is indeed given to the believer, but it was also given so that he might be a believer.

It was therefore quite right for me to say in another place in the same book: "Since it is not from works but by God's mercy that we are called to believe, and that we are enabled to do good once we believe, the Gentiles are not to be begrudged this mercy." Even so, I dealt less carefully there with the calling that takes place through God's purpose.
This book begins thus: "These are the thoughts in the epistle of Paul to the Romans."
CHAPTER 23. EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS, ONE BOOK.

After this book I expounded the same apostle's Epistle to the Galatians. I did not do it piecemeal, passing over some parts, but continuously and in its entirety, and I contained this exposition in one volume.

In it I wrote: "The earlier apostles, then, are truthful, who were sent not from men but by God through a man, namely through Jesus Christ while he was still mortal. The last apostle too is truthful, who was sent after the resurrection through Jesus Christ, now wholly God." The phrase "now wholly God" refers to the immortality that he began to have after the resurrection. It does not refer to his divinity, which is ever immortal. He never departed from that divinity, and in it he was wholly God even when he was still to die. What follows makes this meaning clear, for I went on to say: "The other apostles are the earlier ones, sent through Christ while he was still in part man, that is, mortal. The last is the apostle Paul, sent through Jesus Christ now wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect." I said this because of the apostle's words, "not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father," as though Jesus Christ were no longer a man. For there follows: "who raised him from the dead," which shows why he said "nor through a man." Accordingly, with respect to his immortality, Christ, who is God, is now no longer a man. But with respect to the substance of human nature, in which he ascended into heaven, he is even now "the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." For he will come in the same way as those who saw him going into heaven saw him.

Likewise I said: "It is grace by which our sins are forgiven us so that we may be reconciled to God, but peace by which we are reconciled to God." This should be taken in such a way that we still recognize that both belong to God's grace in the general sense. In the same way, among the people of God, Israel in the specific sense is one thing and Judah another, and yet both are Israel in the general sense.

Again, when I expounded "What then? The law was set forth for the sake of transgression," I thought it should be punctuated so that the question was "What then?" and the answer was "The law was set forth for the sake of transgression." This is indeed not far from the truth. But a better punctuation seems to me to be one in which the question is "What then is the law?" and the answer follows: "It was set forth for the sake of transgression."

I also said: "So, in perfect order, he adds, 'But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the law.' From this we understand that those under the law are those whose spirit lusts against the flesh in such a way that they do not do what they want. That is, they do not keep themselves unconquered in the love of righteousness but are conquered by the flesh that lusts against them." This comes from the way I then understood the saying "The flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want." I took it to apply to those who are under the law and not yet under grace. For I had not yet understood that these words also fit those who are under grace and not under the law. They too have concupiscences of the flesh, against which they lust with the spirit. Though they do not consent to them, they would still prefer not to have them, if they could. Therefore they do not do whatever they want, because they want to be rid of these concupiscences and cannot. For they will be free of them only when they are also free of corruptible flesh.
This book begins thus: "The reason why the apostle writes to the Galatians is this."
CHAPTER 24.
AN UNFINISHED EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, ONE BOOK.

I had also undertaken an exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, as I had of the Epistle to the Galatians. Had this work been completed, it would have run to several books. I finished one of them, which was devoted solely to discussing the greeting itself, from the beginning up to where he says, "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." We lingered over it because we wanted to resolve a most difficult question that came up in our discussion: the question of the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come. But after that I stopped adding further volumes to expound the whole epistle. I was deterred by the size and labour of the work itself and slipped into other, easier tasks. So it came about that I left the first book I had produced standing alone, and I wished its title to be: An Unfinished Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans.

In it I said that grace lies in the forgiveness of sins and peace in reconciliation with God. Wherever I said this, it should not be taken as though peace itself and reconciliation did not belong to grace in the general sense. Rather, the apostle used the name "grace" to signify specifically the forgiveness of sins. In the same way, we speak of "the law" in a specific sense, as in the saying "the law and the prophets," and also in a general sense, in which the prophets too are included.
This book begins thus: "In the epistle which the apostle Paul wrote to the Romans."
CHAPTER 25. EIGHTY-THREE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, ONE BOOK.

Among the things I have written there is also a lengthy work which nevertheless counts as a single book. Its title is *On Eighty-Three Different Questions*. These questions had been scattered over many sheets, because from the very first period of my conversion, after we came to Africa, they were dictated in no particular order, as the brothers asked me about them whenever they saw me free. When I was already a bishop, I had them gathered together and made into one book, with numbers added, so that anyone may easily find what he wants to read.
The first of these questions is: whether the soul exists of itself;
the second, on free will;
the third: whether man becomes worse with God as the author;
the fourth: what is the cause of man becoming worse;
the fifth: whether an irrational animal can be happy;
the sixth, on evil;
the seventh: what is properly called the soul in a living being;
the eighth: whether the soul is moved by itself;

the ninth: whether truth can be perceived by the bodily senses. In it I said: "Everything that a bodily sense reaches, which is also called sensible, is changing without any pause in time." This is certainly not true of the incorruptible bodies of the resurrection; but at present none of our bodily senses reaches them, unless perhaps something of the kind is revealed by God.
The tenth is: whether the body is from God; the eleventh: why Christ was born of a woman.
In the twelfth place, where the title is:

"The opinion of a certain wise man," the piece is not mine. But because some brothers came to know it through me, brothers who happened at that time to be inquiring into these matters with great care, and because they liked it, they wanted to write it down among my questions. It is by a certain Fonteius of Carthage, on purifying the mind in order to see God. He wrote it as a pagan, but he died a baptized Christian.
The thirteenth is: by what proof it is established that human beings surpass beasts;
the fourteenth: that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was not a phantom;
the fifteenth, on understanding;
the sixteenth, on the Son;
the seventeenth, on God's knowledge;
the eighteenth, on the Trinity;
the nineteenth, on God and the creature;
the twentieth, on the place of God;

the twenty-first: whether God is not the author of evil. Here one must take care that what I said is not misunderstood: "He is not the author of evil, because he is the author of all things that exist, since insofar as they exist, they are good." From this it should not be thought that the punishment of the wicked does not come from him, though it is certainly an evil for those who are punished. But I said this in the sense in which it is said, "God did not make death," whereas elsewhere it is written, "Death and life are from the Lord God." So the punishment of the wicked, which comes from God, is indeed an evil for the wicked, but it belongs among the good works of God, since it is just that the wicked should be punished, and certainly everything that is just is good.
The twenty-second is: that God is not subject to necessity.
The twenty-third is: on the Father and the Son. There I said that he begot the Wisdom by which he is called wise; but I dealt with this question better later, in my book on the Trinity.

The twenty-fourth is: whether both sin and right action lie in the free choice of the will. That this is so is entirely true; but for the will to be free to act rightly, it is set free by the grace of God.
The twenty-fifth, on the cross of Christ;
the twenty-sixth, on the difference between sins;
the twenty-seventh, on providence;
the twenty-eighth: why God willed to make the world;
the twenty-ninth: whether there is any up or down in the universe;
the thirtieth: whether all things were created for man's benefit.

The thirty-first is not mine either, but Cicero's. But because the brothers also came to know it through me, they wrote it down among the pieces they were collecting, wishing to know how he divided and defined the virtues of the soul.
The thirty-second is: whether one person can understand a given thing better than another, so that the understanding of the same thing goes on to infinity.
The thirty-third is on fear;
the thirty-fourth: whether nothing else is to be loved than freedom from fear;

the thirty-fifth: what is to be loved. In it I said that what is to be loved is that which to have is nothing other than to know it; I do not fully approve of this. For those to whom it was said, "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" did not lack God; and yet they did not know him, or did not know him as he ought to be known. Likewise, when I said, "No one, then, knows the happy life and is unhappy," by "knows" I meant knows as it ought to be known. For who, at least among those who already use reason, is wholly ignorant of it, since they know that they want to be happy?

The thirty-sixth, on nourishing charity. There I said: "So when God and the soul are loved, it is properly so called [?], most pure and perfect, if nothing else is loved." If this is true, how can the apostle say, "No one ever hated his own flesh," and on that basis urge that wives be loved? But the reason I said "is properly called" is that the flesh is indeed loved, yet not properly, but for the sake of the soul, for whose use it is sufficient. For even if it seems to be loved for its own sake, when we do not want it to be ugly, its beauty must be referred to something else, namely to him from whom all things have their beauty.
The thirty-seventh, on the one who is always born;
the thirty-eighth, on the shaping of the soul;
the thirty-ninth, on food;
the fortieth: since the nature of souls is one, where do the different wills of human beings come from;
the forty-first: since God made all things, why did he not make them equal;
the forty-second: how the Wisdom of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, was both in his mother's womb and in heaven;
the forty-third: why the Son of God appeared in a man and the Holy Spirit in a dove;

the forty-fourth: why the Lord Jesus Christ came so late. There, recalling the ages of the human race as though it were a single man, I said: "Nor was it fitting for a teacher to come from God, by imitating whom the race would be formed in the best way of life, except in the time of its youth." And I added that this is the point of what the apostle says: guarding the little ones under the law as under a tutor. But someone may be troubled by the fact that elsewhere I said that Christ came in the sixth age of the human race, as if in its old age. What was said of youth, then, refers to the vigor and fervor of faith, which works through love; what was said of old age refers to the count of the times. For both can be understood of humanity as a whole, as they can in the ages of individuals. In the body youth and old age cannot exist together, but in the mind they can: the one through eagerness, the other through gravity.
The forty-fifth is: against the astrologers.
The forty-sixth is on the ideas.

The forty-seventh: whether we shall one day be able to see our thoughts. There I said: "Angelic bodies, such as we hope to have, must be believed to be most full of light and ethereal." If this is taken to mean without the members we now have, and without the substance of flesh, though incorruptible, it is a mistake. This question of seeing our thoughts is treated much better in my work *The City of God*.
The forty-eighth, on what is to be believed;
the forty-ninth: why the children of Israel offered visible sacrifices of animal victims;
the fiftieth, on the equality of the Son;

the fifty-first, on man made in the image and likeness of God. There I said: "Clearly a man is not correctly called life." But what of this, when even a man's corpse is called a man? So I ought at least to have said "is not properly called" where I said "is not correctly called." I also said: "Nor is it an unintelligent distinction that the image and likeness of God is one thing, and what is made to the image and likeness of God is another, as we understand man to have been made to the image." This should not be understood as if man is not called the image of God, since the apostle says, "A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God"; but he is also said to be made to the image of God, which is not said of the Only-begotten, who is only the image, not made to the image.
The fifty-second is on the saying: "I regret that I made man";
the fifty-third, on the gold and silver that the Israelites received from the Egyptians;

the fifty-fourth, on the text: "For me it is good to cling to God." There I said: "What is better than every soul, that we call God." It should rather have been said: better than every created spirit.
the fifty-fifth, on the text: "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number";
the fifty-sixth, on the forty-six years of the building of the temple;
the fifty-seventh, on the hundred and fifty-three fish;
the fifty-eighth, on John the Baptist;
the fifty-ninth, on the ten virgins;
the sixtieth: "But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son of Man, but the Father alone";

the sixty-first, on what is written in the Gospel, that the Lord fed the crowds on the mountain with five loaves. There I said: "The two fish signify those two persons, the royal and the priestly, to whom that most holy anointing also belonged." It should rather have been said "especially belonged," since we read that prophets too were sometimes anointed. I also said: "Luke, who presented Christ as the priest ascending after the abolition of sins, ascends to David through Nathan, because the prophet Nathan had been sent, by whose rebuke David obtained through repentance the abolition of his sin." This is not to be taken as if the prophet Nathan were the same person as Nathan the son of David; for I did not say there "because he himself was the prophet sent," but "because the prophet Nathan had been sent," so that the mystery is understood to lie not in the same man but in the same name.

The sixty-second is on what is written in the Gospel, that Jesus baptized more than John, although he himself did not baptize, but his disciples. There I spoke of "that thief to whom it was said, 'Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise,' who had not even received baptism." I find indeed that other rulers of the holy Church before us also stated this in their writings; but by what proofs it can be shown that the thief was not baptized, I do not know. This matter is discussed more carefully in some of my later works, especially in the one I wrote to Vincentius Victor on the origin of the soul.
The sixty-third is on the Word;
the sixty-fourth, on the Samaritan woman;
the sixty-fifth, on the raising of Lazarus;

the sixty-sixth, on the passage: "Do you not know, brothers (for I am speaking to those who know the law), that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives?" up to the place where it is written: "He will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you." There, wishing to explain what the apostle says, "We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal," I said: "That is, I consent to the flesh, not yet set free by spiritual grace." This is not to be taken as though a spiritual person, already living under grace, could not also say this of himself, and the rest, up to the place where it is said, "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?" I learned this later, as I have already acknowledged. Again, explaining what the apostle says, "The body indeed is dead because of sin," I said: "He calls the body dead as long as it is such that its need for temporal things troubles the mind." But later it seemed better to me that the body was called dead because it now bears the necessity of dying, which it did not have before sin.

The sixty-seventh is on the passage: "For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come that will be revealed in us," up to what is said: "For in hope we were saved." There, explaining the text, "And the creation itself will be set free from the bondage of decay," I said: "'And the creation itself,' that is, man himself, when, having lost the seal of the image through sin, he remained merely a creature." This is not to be taken as if man lost everything he had of the image of God. For if he had not lost it at all, there would be no reason for saying, "Be renewed in the newness of your mind," and, "We are being transformed into the same image"; but again, if he had lost it entirely, nothing would remain to justify the saying, "Although man walks in the image, yet he is troubled in vain." Likewise, what I said, that the highest angels live spiritually and the lowest animally, was said of the lowest more boldly than can be shown either from the holy Scriptures or from the facts themselves; for even if perhaps it can be shown, it can be shown only with the greatest difficulty.

The sixty-eighth is on the text: "O man, who are you to answer back to God?" There I said: "Even if someone, with lighter sins, or certainly with graver and many sins, yet through much groaning and the sorrow of repentance becomes worthy of God's mercy, it will not be his own doing (for if he were left to himself he would perish), but that of the merciful God, who comes to the aid of his prayers and sorrow. For it is not enough to will unless God has mercy; but God, who calls to peace, does not have mercy unless the will has gone before toward peace." This was said of what follows repentance. For there is also a mercy of God that goes before the will itself; if there were not, the will would not be prepared by the Lord. To that mercy belongs the calling itself, which goes before even faith. Speaking of this a little later, I said: "But this calling, which works at fitting times, whether in individual persons or in peoples or in the human race itself, will belong to a high and deep ordering." To this also belong the texts: "In the womb I sanctified you," and "When you were in your father's loins I saw you," and "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated," and the rest. But as for the text "When you were in your father's loins I saw you," I do not know how it came to my mind as though it were written in Scripture.
the sixty-ninth, on the text: "Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him";

the seventieth, on what the apostle says: "Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your struggle? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law";
the seventy-first, on the text: "Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ";
the seventy-second, on eternal times;
the seventy-third, on the text: "And found in appearance as a man";
the seventy-fourth, on what is written in Paul's letter to the Colossians: "In whom we have redemption for the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God";
the seventy-fifth, on the inheritance of God;
the seventy-sixth, on what the apostle James says: "Do you want to know, you empty man, that faith without works is idle?"
the seventy-seventh, on fear: whether it is a sin;
the seventy-eighth, on the beauty of idols;
the seventy-ninth: why Pharaoh's magicians performed miracles as Moses, the servant of God, did;
the eightieth, against the Apollinarians;
the eighty-first, on the forty days and the fifty days;
the eighty-second, on the text: "For the Lord reproves the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives";
the eighty-third, on marriage.
This work begins thus: "Whether the soul exists of itself."
CHAPTER 26. ON LYING, ONE BOOK.

I also wrote a book on lying. Although it takes some effort to understand, it offers useful exercise for the intellect and mind, and does even more for character by fostering a love of truthful speech. I had decided to remove this one too from my works, because it seemed to me obscure, convoluted and altogether tiresome, and for that reason I had not published it. Then, after I later wrote another book entitled *Against Lying*, I was all the more determined that this one should cease to exist, and I had ordered this, but it was not done. So when, in this review of my works, I found it still intact, I directed that it too should remain, now that it has been reviewed, especially because it contains some necessary things that are not in the other. The reason the other is titled *Against Lying* and this one *On Lying* is that the former is from beginning to end an open attack on lying, while a large part of this one is taken up with a discussion that inquires into the question; yet both are directed to the same end.
This book begins thus: "There is a great question about lying."
CHAPTER 27. TO SIMPLICIANUS, TWO BOOKS.

Of the books I produced as a bishop, the first two are addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of the church of Milan, who succeeded the most blessed Ambrose. They deal with various questions, two of which, taken from the apostle Paul's letter to the Romans, I put into the first book.

The first of these concerns the passage: "What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means," up to where he says: "Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord." In it I explained the apostle's words, "The law is spiritual, but I am carnal," and the rest, which show the flesh fighting against the spirit, as though they describe a man still under the law and not yet living under grace. Only long afterward did I realize that these words can also be those of a spiritual man, and that this is the more probable view.

The second question in this book runs from the place where he says, "And not only so, but also Rebecca, having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father," up to where he says, "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." In solving this question I did indeed labor on behalf of the free choice of the human will, but the grace of God prevailed; and I could only arrive at the conclusion that the apostle is understood to have spoken with the clearest truth when he said, "For who makes you different? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" The martyr Cyprian, wishing to show this too, summed it all up in a single heading, saying: "We must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own."

In the second book the remaining questions are treated and, as far as my small ability allowed, resolved. They all concern the scripture called Kingdoms. The first of them is on the text: "And the Spirit of the Lord leapt upon

Saul," whereas elsewhere it is said: "And an evil spirit of the Lord was upon Saul." In explaining it I said: "Although what one wills is in each person's power, what one is able to do is not in anyone's power." This was said because we do not call anything "in our power" except what happens when we will it; and there, first and foremost, is willing itself. For the will itself is present without any interval of time when we will. But this power, too, the power to live well, we receive from above, when the will is prepared by the Lord.
The second question is: how it was said, "I regret that I made Saul king"; the third:
whether the unclean spirit that was in the medium could have brought it about that Samuel was seen by Saul and spoke with him;
the fourth, on the text: "King David went in and sat before the Lord";
the fifth, on what Elijah said: "O Lord, witness of this widow with whom I am staying, you have done evil in killing her son."
This work begins thus: "Most welcome indeed and most pleasing."
CHAPTER 28.
AGAINST THE LETTER OF MANI CALLED "THE FOUNDATION," ONE BOOK.

The book against the letter of Mani called "The Foundation" refutes only its opening sections. But on the other parts of the letter I attached notes, where it seemed fitting, by which the whole of it is overturned, and which would remind me if I should ever have time to write against the whole.
This book begins thus: "The one true almighty God."
CHAPTER 29.
ON THE CONTEST, ONE BOOK.
The book *On the Christian Contest* was written in a plain style for brothers not well schooled in the Latin language. It contains the rule of faith and precepts for living.

In it there is the following statement: "Nor let us listen to those who deny the future resurrection of the flesh and cite what the apostle Paul says, 'Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,' not understanding what the same apostle says: 'This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality'; for when this has happened, there will no longer be flesh and blood, but a heavenly body." This is not to be taken as though the substance of the flesh will not exist. Rather, the apostle must be understood to have used the name "flesh and blood" for the corruption itself of flesh and blood, which will certainly not exist in that kingdom, where the flesh will be incorruptible. It can, however, also be understood in another way: that by "flesh and blood" the apostle meant the works of flesh and blood, and that those who persist in loving these will not possess the kingdom of God.
This book begins thus: "The crown of victory."
CHAPTER 30. ON CHRISTIAN TEACHING, FOUR BOOKS.

When I found that the books On Christian Teaching were unfinished, I chose to complete them rather than leave them as they were and move on to reviewing other works. So I completed the third book, which had been written up to the place where the gospel passage is cited about the woman who hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened. I also added a final book, and so completed the work in four books. The first three help the reader to understand the Scriptures, and the fourth shows how what we understand should be presented.

In the second book I said that the book many call the Wisdom of Solomon was also written by Jesus son of Sirach, like Ecclesiasticus. I later learned that this is not as certain as I stated, and I have found it altogether more probable that he is not its author.

Where I said, "With these forty-four books the authority of the Old Testament is concluded," I used the term "Old Testament" according to the way the Church now speaks. The Apostle, however, seems to use "old testament" only for what was given on Mount Sinai.

I also said that Saint Ambrose had solved the question from the history of the times, as though Plato and Jeremiah had been contemporaries. Here my memory deceived me. What that bishop said on this matter can be read in the book he wrote on the sacraments, or on philosophy.
This work begins thus: "There are certain rules."
CHAPTER 31. AGAINST THE PARTY OF DONATUS, TWO BOOKS.
There are two books of mine entitled Against the Party of Donatus.

In the first of these books I said that I did not approve of forcing schismatics into communion by the pressure of any secular power. At that time I truly did not approve of it, because I had not yet learned by experience how much evil their impunity would dare, or how much careful discipline could do to change them for the better.
This work begins thus: "Since the Donatists to us."
CHAPTER 32. THE CONFESSIONS, THIRTEEN BOOKS.

The thirteen books of my Confessions praise God, who is just and good, for both my evil deeds and my good ones, and they stir up the human mind and heart toward him. For my own part, they had this effect on me while they were being written, and they still have it when they are read. What others think of them is their own affair. Yet I know that they have greatly pleased many brothers and still please them. The first to the tenth books were written about me. The remaining three are about the Holy Scriptures, from the words "In the beginning God made heaven and earth" to the rest of the Sabbath.

In the fourth book I was confessing the misery of my soul at the death of a friend, and said that our soul had in a certain way been made one out of two. Then I said: "And perhaps that is why I feared to die, lest he whom I had loved so much should die completely." This seems to me more a light piece of rhetoric than a serious confession, although the foolishness is somewhat softened by the added word "perhaps."
In the thirteenth book I said that the firmament was made between the higher, spiritual waters and the lower, bodily waters. I said this without enough thought, and the matter is very obscure.
This work begins thus: "Great are you, O Lord."
CHAPTER 33.
AGAINST FAUSTUS THE MANICHEAN, THIRTY-THREE BOOKS.

Faustus the Manichean blasphemed the Law and the Prophets, their God, and the incarnation of Christ. He also said that the Scriptures of the New Testament, which refute him, had been falsified. Against him I wrote a large work, setting out his words and giving my replies. There are thirty-three disputations, and why should I not call them books? Some of them are short, but they are still books. One of them, in which I defend the life of the patriarchs against his accusations, is longer than almost any other book of mine.

In the third book I was solving the question of how Joseph could have had two fathers. I said that he was born of one and adopted by the other, but I should also have stated what kind of adoption it was. As I put it, it sounds as though the other father adopted him while still alive. But the Law also adopted sons for the dead. It commanded that when a man died without sons, his brother should marry the widow and raise up offspring by her for the dead brother. This certainly gives a simpler account of how one man had two fathers. The brothers in this case were half-brothers born of the same mother. When one of them, called Heli, died, the other, Jacob, married his wife. Matthew says that Joseph was begotten by Jacob. But Jacob begot him for his half-brother, and Luke says Joseph was Heli's son, not by birth, of course, but by adoption under the Law. This was found in the writings of people who wrote about the matter within living memory of the Lord's ascension. Africanus even records the name of the woman involved. By her first husband Matthan, who according to Matthew was Jacob's father and Joseph's grandfather, she bore Jacob, the father of Joseph. By her later husband Melchi she bore Heli, whose adopted son Joseph was. I had not yet read this when I was answering Faustus, but I could not doubt that through adoption one man could have two fathers.
In the twelfth and thirteenth books I discussed Noah's second son, called Ham, as though his father had cursed him in his own person. But Scripture shows that he was cursed in his son Canaan.

In the fourteenth book things are said about the sun and the moon as though they had feelings and therefore put up with their foolish worshipers. Still, the words there can be taken as transferred from living to lifeless things by the figure of speech called in Greek metaphor. In the same way it is written that the sea rages in its mother's womb, wanting to come forth, although it certainly has no will.

In the twenty-ninth book I said: "Far be it that there should be anything shameful in the members of the saints, even the genital ones. They are indeed called unseemly because they lack the kind of beauty of the members that are placed in plain view." But later, in other writings of mine, I gave a more probable reason why the Apostle too called them unseemly. It is because of the law in the members that fights against the law of the mind. That law came about through sin, not from the original making of our nature.
This work begins thus: "There was a certain Faustus."
CHAPTER 34. AGAINST FELIX THE MANICHEAN, TWO BOOKS.

For two days I debated in church, before the people, against a Manichean named Felix. He had come to Hippo to sow that same error. He was one of their teachers, and though he had no training in the liberal arts, he was more cunning than Fortunatus. The record is a set of church proceedings, but it is counted among my books. So there are two books. The second discusses the free choice of the will, whether to do evil or good. Scripture says of some, "If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free." Given the sort of man we were dealing with, we were under no need to discuss more carefully the grace by which such people become truly free.
This work begins thus: "In the sixth consulship of Honorius Augustus, on the seventh day before the Ides of December."
CHAPTER 35.
ON THE NATURE OF THE GOOD, ONE BOOK.

The book On the Nature of the Good is against the Manicheans. It shows that God is the unchangeable nature and the highest good. All other natures, whether spiritual or bodily, come from him, and all of them are good insofar as they are natures. It also shows what evil is and where it comes from. Finally, it shows how many evils the Manicheans place in the nature of the good, and how many goods in the nature of evil, both of which natures their error has invented.
This book begins thus: "The highest good, than which there is nothing higher, is God."
CHAPTER 36. AGAINST SECUNDINUS THE MANICHEAN, ONE BOOK.

A certain Secundinus wrote to me. He was not one of those whom the Manicheans call the elect, but one of those they call hearers, and I did not even know him by sight. He wrote as a friend and reproached me respectfully for attacking that heresy in my writings. He warned me not to do so and urged me instead to follow it, defending it and criticizing the Catholic faith. I answered him. But at the head of that little work I did not state who was writing to whom, so it is to be counted among my books rather than my letters. His letter is also copied there at the beginning. The title of this volume of mine is Against Secundinus the Manichean. In my judgment it is better than anything else I have been able to write against that plague.
This book begins thus: "The goodwill toward me that appears in your letter."
CHAPTER 37.
AGAINST HILARUS, ONE BOOK.

Meanwhile a certain Hilarus, a man of tribune's rank and a Catholic layman, had become angry with the ministers of God, as often happens, though I do not know why. At that time a custom had begun at Carthage of singing hymns from the book of Psalms at the altar, either before the offering or while the offering was being distributed to the people. Hilarus attacked this custom with abusive criticism wherever he could, claiming that it ought not to be done. At the brothers' request I answered him, and the book is called Against Hilarus.
This book begins thus: "Those who say that mention of the Old Testament."
CHAPTER 38.
QUESTIONS ON THE GOSPELS, TWO BOOKS.

There are some explanations of certain passages from the Gospel according to Matthew, and others likewise from the Gospel according to Luke. The first were gathered into one book and the second into another. The title of this work is Questions on the Gospels. My prologue explains well enough why only these passages of those evangelists were explained in these books, and which passages they are. The questions are attached to the prologue and numbered, so that anyone can follow the numbers and find what he wants to read.
In the first book it is stated that the Lord told two disciples privately about his passion. A faulty manuscript misled us here, for the text says "twelve," not "two."

In the second book I did not want to explain how Joseph, whose wife is called the Virgin Mary, could have had two fathers. One common explanation is that a brother married the wife of his dead brother to raise up offspring for him according to the Law. I called this explanation weak, because the Law commanded the child to take the dead man's name. That is not true. When the Law spoke of the dead man's name, it meant that the child should be called his son, not that he should be called by the same name.
This work begins thus: "This work has not been written in such a way."
CHAPTER 39. NOTES ON JOB, ONE BOOK.

There is a book entitled Notes on Job. I could not easily say whether it should be considered mine, or rather the work of those who copied the notes from the margins of the manuscript and gathered them into a single body as well as they could or would. The notes please the very few who understand them, yet even these readers are bound to be put off by much that they do not understand. In many places even the words being explained have not been copied in a way that makes clear what is being explained. Then the statements are so brief, and so obscure as a result, that a reader can hardly bear it, since he has to pass over a great deal without understanding it. Finally, I found the work itself so full of errors in our manuscripts that I could not correct it. I would not want it said to have been published by me, except that I know the brothers have it, and it could not be refused to their eagerness.
This book begins thus: "And his works were great upon the earth."
CHAPTER 40.
ON CATECHIZING THE UNINSTRUCTED, ONE BOOK.

There is also one book On Catechizing the Uninstructed, which bears this very title. In it I said: "Nor did the angel who, together with the other spirits who followed him, abandoned obedience to God through pride and became the devil, do any harm to God, but only to himself. For God knows how to set in order souls that abandon him." It would have been more fitting to say "spirits that abandon him," since I was speaking of angels.
This book begins thus: "You asked me, brother Deogratias."
CHAPTER 41. ON THE TRINITY, FIFTEEN BOOKS.

I wrote fifteen books on the Trinity, which is God, over a number of years. I had not yet finished twelve of them and was keeping them longer than those who eagerly wanted to have them could bear. They were taken from me before I had corrected them as well as I should and could have done when I meant to publish them. When I learned of this, since I still had other copies, I decided not to publish them myself at all. I would simply keep them and tell in some other work of mine what had happened to me with them. But the brothers pressed me, and I could not resist them. So I corrected the books as far as I thought they needed correcting, completed them, and published them. At the beginning I attached a letter I wrote to the venerable Aurelius, bishop of the church of Carthage. In that letter, as a kind of prologue, I explained what had happened, what I had planned to do on my own judgment, and what I had done under the pressure of the brothers' love.

In the eleventh of these books, when I was discussing the visible body, I said: "Therefore to love it is to become estranged." This refers to the kind of love in which a person loves something so that he thinks he will be happy by enjoying it. To love bodily beauty to the praise of the Creator is not to become estranged, provided that one is truly happy by enjoying the Creator himself.

In the same book I said: "Nor do I remember a four-footed bird, because I have never seen one. Yet I picture one very easily when I take a winged form such as I have seen and add two more feet such as I have likewise seen." When I said this I failed to recall the four-footed flying creatures that the Law mentions. The Law does not count as feet the two hind legs with which locusts leap. It calls locusts clean, and so distinguishes them from unclean flying creatures of this sort that do not leap with such legs, such as beetles. All flying creatures of this kind are called four-footed in the Law.
In the twelfth book there is a kind of explanation of the Apostle's words where he says:

"Every sin that a man commits is outside the body." That explanation does not satisfy me. Nor do I think the words "But he who commits fornication sins against his own body" should be understood to mean anyone who acts in order to obtain things perceived through the body, so as to make them the goal of his good. That would cover far more sins than the fornication committed by unlawful intercourse, and it is clear that the Apostle was speaking of the latter when he said this.
Apart from the letter that was later attached at its head, this work begins thus: "Whoever is going to read what we discuss concerning the Trinity."
CHAPTER 42. ON THE HARMONY OF THE EVANGELISTS, FOUR BOOKS.
