During the same years in which I was gradually dictating the books on the Trinity, I also worked continually on other writings, fitting them into the intervals between those books. Among them are the four books On the Harmony of the Evangelists. I wrote them because of people who slander the evangelists as if they disagreed with one another. The first of these books was written against those who honor Christ as a supremely wise man, or pretend to. These people refuse to believe the Gospel because Christ did not write it himself. It was written by his disciples, who in their view mistakenly gave him the divinity that led people to believe he was God.

In that book I said that the Hebrew nation began with Abraham. It is indeed credible that the Hebrews were so named as though they were "Abrahews." But it is more accurate to understand that they were named after the man called Heber, as though they were "Heberews." I have discussed this sufficiently in the sixteenth book of The City of God.

In the second book, discussing Joseph's two fathers, I said that he was begotten by one and adopted by the other. I should have said "adopted for the other." It is more likely that he had been adopted according to the Law for the one who had died, since the man who begot him had married his mother, the widow of his dead brother.

I also said: "Luke, however, traces the line up to David himself through Nathan, the prophet through whom God expiated David's sin." I should have said "through a prophet of that name," so that no one would think they were the same man. They were different men, although the son of David also bore this name.
This work begins thus: "Among all the divine authorities."
CHAPTER 43. AGAINST THE LETTER OF PARMENIAN, THREE BOOKS.

Parmenian was the Donatist bishop of Carthage and the successor of Donatus. In some books against his letter, a new question is treated and resolved: whether the wicked defile the good when both are in unity and share in the same sacraments. These books argue that the wicked do not defile them. The question is raised because of the Church spread throughout the whole world, which the Donatists slandered in order to make their schism.

In the third of these books I discussed how to understand the Apostle's words "Remove the evil from among yourselves." There I said that each person should remove evil from himself. That is not how the words should be understood. They mean rather that the evil person should be removed from among the good, which is done through church discipline. The Greek shows this, because it is written there without ambiguity so as to mean "the evil man," not "this evil." Even so, I also used this interpretation in answering Parmenian.
This work begins thus: "Many things indeed elsewhere against the Donatists."
CHAPTER 44.
ON BAPTISM, SEVEN BOOKS.

The Donatists try to defend themselves by the authority of the most blessed bishop and martyr Cyprian. Against them I wrote seven books On Baptism. In them I showed that nothing works so well as Cyprian's letters and conduct to refute the Donatists and silence them completely, so that they cannot defend their schism against the Catholic Church.

Wherever in these books I spoke of the Church as having no spot or wrinkle, this should not be taken to mean that she is already so. It means that she is being prepared to be so when she appears in glory. For now, because of the ignorance and weakness of some of her members, the whole Church has reason to say every day: "Forgive us our debts."
In the fourth book I said that martyrdom could take the place of baptism. The example I gave of the thief was not really suitable, because it is uncertain whether he was unbaptized.

In the seventh book I followed Cyprian's view of the vessels of gold and silver in a great house. He took these to mean the good, and the wooden and earthen vessels to mean the wicked. He applied the words "some for honor" to the first group, and "others for dishonor" to the second. But I prefer what I later found, or noticed, in Tyconius. In his view, some vessels in both groups are for honor, not only the gold and silver ones, and some in both groups are for dishonor, not only the wooden and earthen ones.
This work begins thus: "In those books which, against the letter of Parmenian."
CHAPTER 45.
AGAINST WHAT CENTURIUS BROUGHT FROM THE DONATISTS, ONE BOOK.

We were dealing with the party of Donatus on many points in frequent debates. During that time a layman who belonged to them then brought to the church some things they had said or written against us. These took the form of a few proof texts, as it were, which they think support their cause. I answered very briefly. The title of this little book is Against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists, and it begins thus: "You say, because it is written in Solomon, 'Abstain from another's water.'"
CHAPTER 46.
TO THE INQUIRIES OF JANUARIUS, TWO BOOKS.

The two books entitled To the Inquiries of Januarius contain many discussions about sacred rites. Some of these the Church observes everywhere, and others only in certain places, that is, not equally everywhere. Not everything could be covered, but the questions asked were answered well enough. The first of these books is a letter, since it states at its head who is writing to whom. This work is nonetheless counted among the books because the second book, which does not bear our names, is much longer and deals with many more matters.

In the first book I said of the manna that it tasted in each person's mouth like whatever he wished. I cannot think how this could be proved, except from the book of Wisdom, which the Jews do not accept as canonical. Even so, this could have been true for the faithful. It could not have been true for those who grumbled against God, since they would surely not have longed for other food if the manna had tasted to them of whatever they wanted.
This work begins thus: "To the questions you asked me."
CHAPTER 47. ON THE WORK OF MONKS, ONE BOOK.

I was compelled to write a book On the Work of Monks by the following situation. When monasteries had begun to appear at Carthage, some monks supported themselves with their own hands in obedience to the Apostle. Others wanted to live on the offerings of the devout and did no work to provide or make up their necessities. They thought, and boasted, that they were the ones fulfilling the apostolic command, citing the place where the Lord says: "Look at the birds of the sky and the lilies of the field." As a result, even among lay people who followed a less demanding way of life but were fervent in zeal, turbulent disputes began to arise. These disturbed the Church, with some defending one view and some the other. In addition, some of those who said that monks should not work wore their hair long. So the quarrels grew, with one side wrangling and the other fighting, as it were, for the interests of their parties. For this reason the venerable old man Aurelius, bishop of the church of that city, ordered me to write something on the matter, and I did.
This book begins thus: "To your command, holy brother Aurelius."
CHAPTER 48.
ON THE GOOD OF MARRIAGE, ONE BOOK.

The heresy of Jovinian, by putting the merit of consecrated virgins on the same level as chastity in marriage, became so influential in the city of Rome that he was said to have driven into marriage even some nuns whose chastity had never before been suspected. His main argument was to press them, saying: "Are you better, then, than Sarah, better than Susanna or Anna?" He also named the other women whom the testimony of holy Scripture commends most highly, women the nuns could not imagine themselves better than or even equal to. In the same way he was also breaking down the holy celibacy of holy men by pointing to the married patriarchs and comparing them. The holy church there resisted this monstrous teaching most faithfully and most bravely. Yet his arguments had lingered in the gossip and whispers of some people, though no one dared to promote them openly. Even poisons creeping about in secret had to be countered, with whatever ability the Lord gave, especially because people were boasting that Jovinian could only have been answered by disparaging marriage, not by praising it. For this reason I published a book entitled On the Good of Marriage. In it I postponed a great question: how children would have been born before human beings deserved death by sinning, since sexual intercourse seems to belong to mortal bodies. I think this question is explained well enough in other writings of mine later on.

In one place I also said: "What food is to the health of the body, intercourse is to the health of the race, and neither is without carnal pleasure. Yet this pleasure, when it is moderated and restrained by temperance and brought back to its natural use, cannot be lust." I said this because lust is not the same thing as the good and right use of lust. Just as it is bad to use good things badly, so it is good to use bad things well. I have discussed this matter more carefully elsewhere, especially against the new Pelagian heretics. As for what I said about Abraham:

"Out of this obedience father Abraham, who was not without a wife, was ready to be without his only son, and slain by his own hand": I do not entirely approve of this. Rather, we should believe that he believed his son, if slain, would soon have been given back to him by resurrection, as we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews.
This book begins as follows: "Since every human being is part of the human race."
Chapter 49. On Holy Virginity, One Book.

After I had written On the Good of Marriage, people expected me to write on holy virginity. I did not put it off. In one volume I showed as well as I could how great a gift of God virginity is, and with how much humility it must be guarded.
This book begins as follows: "We recently published a book On the Good of Marriage."
Chapter 50.
On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, Twelve Books.

About the same time I wrote twelve books on Genesis, from the beginning up to the point where Adam was sent out of paradise and a flaming sword was placed to guard the way to the tree of life. When eleven books had been finished up to that point, I added a twelfth, in which paradise is discussed more carefully. These books are entitled On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, that is, not according to allegorical meanings but according to the actual nature of the events. In this work more questions were asked than answers found. Of the answers found, fewer were settled, and the rest were set out as matters still to be investigated. I began these books after On the Trinity but finished them before it, so I have now reviewed them in the order in which I began them.

In the fifth book, and wherever else in these books I wrote that the seed to whom the promise was made was "ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator," that is not what the apostle says, as I later found when I examined more accurate manuscripts, especially Greek ones. The words were said of the law, but many Latin manuscripts have them as said of the seed, through a translator's error.

In the sixth book I said that Adam lost by sin the image of God in which he was made. This should not be taken to mean that no trace of the image remained in him, but that it had become so disfigured that it needed to be formed anew.

In the twelfth book, concerning the underworld, I think I ought rather to have taught that it is under the earth than to have given reasons why it is believed or said to be under the earth, as though it were not so.
This work begins as follows: "All of divine Scripture is twofold."
Chapter 51. Against the Letter of Petilian, Three Books.

Before I had finished the books On the Trinity and the books On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, I was suddenly faced with the need to answer the letter that Petilian the Donatist had written against the Catholic Church. I could not put this off, and I wrote three volumes on the matter. In the first I answered, as quickly and as truthfully as I could, the first part of the letter he had written to his own people, since the whole letter had not reached us, only a small first part of it. This first volume is itself a letter, addressed to our people, but it is counted among the books because the other two, on the same subject, are books. Later we found the whole letter, and I answered it as carefully as I had answered Faustus the Manichaean: I first set out his words piece by piece under his name, and then my reply to each point under mine. But what I had written before we found the whole letter reached Petilian first. In his anger he tried to answer it, saying whatever he pleased against me personally but failing completely on the actual issue. This could very easily be seen by comparing what each of us wrote, but for the sake of slower readers I took care to show it myself in a reply. That is how a third book was added to this work of mine.
In the first book this work begins as follows: "You know that we have often wished." In the second: "To the first parts of Petilian's letter." In the third: "I have read your letter, Petilian."
Chapter 52.
To Cresconius, a Grammarian of the Party of Donatus, Four Books.

A certain Cresconius, a Donatist grammarian, came across my letter refuting the first parts of Petilian's letter, the parts that had then come into our hands. He thought he ought to answer me, and he wrote his reply to me personally. I answered this work of his in four books, though I had covered everything a complete reply required in three. But I saw that everything he wrote could be answered from the case of the Maximianists alone. The Donatists had condemned the Maximianists as schismatics from their own party, yet they took some of them back with their former ranks, and they did not repeat the baptism these men had given outside their communion. So I added a fourth book as well, in which I showed this very point as carefully and clearly as I could. By the time I wrote these four books, the Emperor Honorius had already issued laws against the Donatists.
This work begins as follows: "Not knowing when my writings might reach you, Cresconius."
Chapter 53. Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists, One Book.

After this I took care to gather the documents needed against the Donatists' error and in support of Catholic truth, from church records, public records and the canonical Scriptures, so that they might reach the Donatists. First I sent them a promise of these documents, so that they themselves might, if possible, ask for them. When this promise came into the hands of some of them, someone or other appeared who wrote against it without giving his name, calling himself "a Donatist" as though that were his name. I wrote another book in reply to him. The documents I had promised I joined to the booklet in which I had promised them, and I wanted the two to make one book. I published it in such a way that it was first posted on the walls of the basilica that had belonged to the Donatists, to be read there. Its title is Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists.

In this book I did not place the acquittal of Felix of Abthugni, who consecrated Caecilian, in the order that later became clear to me after carefully examining the consular dates. I placed it as though he had been acquitted after Caecilian, whereas it took place before.

There is also this. After citing the testimony of the apostle Jude, where he says, "These are the ones who separate themselves, worldly people, not having the Spirit," I added: "Of whom the apostle Paul also says, 'But the worldly person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God.'" But these people are not to be equated with those whom schism has cut off from the Church altogether. The same apostle Paul says that the former are little children in Christ, who are not yet able to take solid food but whom he still nourishes with milk. The others, however, are to be counted not among little children but among the dead and the lost, so that if any of them is corrected and united to the Church, it can rightly be said of him: "He was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and is found."
This book begins as follows: "You who are afraid to agree with the Catholic Church."
Chapter 54. Against an Unknown Donatist, One Book.
I wanted the other book, which I mentioned above, to have the title Against an Unknown Donatist.
Here too the true chronological order regarding the acquittal of Caecilian's consecrator is not given.

Also, when I said, "to the multitude of tares, by which all heresies are understood," a necessary conjunction is missing. I should have said, "by which all heresies too are understood" [or: "by which all heresies as well are understood"]. As it stands, it sounds as though the tares are only outside the Church and not also within the Church. Yet the Church is itself the kingdom of Christ, from which his angels will gather all causes of sin at harvest time. That is why the martyr Cyprian says: "Even if there seem to be tares in the Church, neither our faith nor our love should be hindered, so that because we see tares in the Church we ourselves withdraw from the Church." I have defended this view elsewhere too, and above all at the conference, against these same Donatists face to face.
This book begins as follows: "We promised proofs of the necessary matters, collected in a brief summary."
Chapter 55.
A Warning to the Donatists about the Maximianists, One Book.

I saw that the labor of reading kept many people from learning how completely the party of Donatus lacks reason and truth. So I wrote a very short booklet, in which I thought it best to warn them about the Maximianists alone. Being easy to copy, it could come into the hands of more people, and being short, it could more easily be committed to memory. I gave it the title A Warning to the Donatists about the Maximianists.
This book begins as follows: "All of you who are troubled by people's slanders and accusations."
Chapter 56. On the Divination of Demons, One Book.
About the same time, a discussion made it necessary for me to write a booklet on the divination of demons, and that is its title.

In one passage of it I said that demons sometimes learn with complete ease the intentions of human beings, not only those spoken aloud but also those conceived in thought, when certain signs from the mind are expressed in the body. Here I asserted something very obscure more boldly than I should have. It has indeed been found through a number of experiences that such things come to the knowledge of demons. But whether certain signs are given off by the body of people thinking, signs perceptible to demons but hidden from us, or whether demons know these things by some other power, a spiritual one, is something human beings can find out only with great difficulty, or not at all.
This book begins as follows: "One day during the holy days of the octave."
Chapter 57.
Six Questions Explained against the Pagans.

Meanwhile six questions were sent to me from Carthage, put forward by a friend whom I wished to see become a Christian, to be resolved against the pagans, especially since he said some of them had been put forward by the philosopher Porphyry. But I do not think this is Porphyry the Sicilian, whose fame is so great. I gathered my discussions of these questions into one book, not a long one, entitled Six Questions Explained against the Pagans. The first is about the resurrection; the second about the time when the Christian religion appeared; the third about the distinction between sacrifices; the fourth about the saying, "With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you"; the fifth about the Son of God according to Solomon; the sixth about the prophet Jonah.

In the second of these I said: "The salvation offered by this religion, the only true one, through which alone true salvation is truly promised, was never lacking to anyone who was worthy of it, and anyone to whom it was lacking was not worthy." I did not say this as though anyone were worthy by his own merits. I meant it in the sense in which the apostle says that it was not from works but from him who calls that the words were spoken, "The elder will serve the younger," a calling he declares belongs to God's purpose. So he says, "not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace"; and again, "We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose." Of this calling he says, "that he may count you worthy of his holy calling."
After the letter that was later added at the beginning, this book begins as follows: "Some people are troubled, and ask."
Chapter 58. An Exposition of the Epistle of James to the Twelve Tribes.

Among my short works I found an exposition of the Epistle of James. On reviewing it, I saw that it is really a set of notes explaining certain passages of the epistle, which the brothers diligently gathered into a book because they did not want them to remain in the margins of the manuscript. So they are of some help, except that the text of the epistle we were reading when I dictated them had not been carefully translated from the Greek.
This book begins as follows: "To the twelve tribes in the dispersion, greetings."
Chapter 59.
On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, and on the Baptism of Infants, to Marcellinus, Three Books.

Then necessity compelled me to write against the Pelagian heresy as well. Until then, when it was needed, we had dealt with it not in writing but in sermons and conversations, as each of us could or ought. So when their questions were sent to me from Carthage for me to resolve in writing, I first wrote three books entitled On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins.

In them I discuss mainly the baptism of infants because of original sin, and the grace by which we are justified, that is, made righteous, although in this life no one keeps the commandments of righteousness so perfectly that he does not need to pray for his sins and say, "Forgive us our debts." It was by holding views contrary to all this that these people founded a new heresy. In these books, however, I judged that their names should still be [?withheld], hoping that they could be corrected more easily that way. Indeed, in the third book, which is a letter but is counted among the books because of the two I thought it should be joined to, I even mentioned Pelagius himself by name, not without some praise, because many people spoke highly of his life. And I refuted those of his views that he set down in his writings not in his own person but as an account of what others were saying, views which later, now a heretic, he defended with the most stubborn animosity. His disciple Caelestius, however, had already been excommunicated for such assertions at Carthage in a court of bishops, at which I was not present.

In one passage of the second book I said: "This will be granted to some even at the end, that through a sudden change they will not feel death," leaving room for a more careful inquiry into the matter. For either they will not die, or else, passing from this life into death and from death into eternal life by a very swift change, as in the twinkling of an eye, they will not feel death.
This work begins as follows: "Although amid great and surging cares."
Chapter 60.
On the One Baptism, against Petilian, to Constantine, One Book.

At that time a friend of mine received a book On the One Baptism from some Donatist presbyter, who said that it had been written by Petilian, their bishop of Constantina. My friend brought it to me and urgently asked me to answer it. I wanted my own book, in which I answered it, to have the same title, namely On the One Baptism.

In that book I said that when the Donatists brought charges against Felix of Abthugni, who consecrated Caecilian, the Emperor Constantine did not refuse to give the accusation a hearing, although he had already found them to be slanderers bringing false charges against Caecilian. Later, when the chronological order was examined, this was found to be otherwise. The emperor first had Felix's case heard by the proconsul, where we read that Felix was acquitted. Afterwards he himself heard Caecilian together with his accusers and found him innocent, and it was then that he found them to be slanderers in their charges against him. This chronological order, established by the consular dates, refutes and overturns the Donatists' slanders in this case far more forcefully, as I have shown elsewhere.
This book begins as follows: "To answer those who hold opposing views."
Chapter 61. On the Maximianists, against the Donatists, One Book.

Among my other works against the Donatists I also wrote a book that was not very short, like the earlier one, but long and much more thorough. It shows how the case of the Maximianists alone, a schism that arose from within the party of Donatus itself, completely overturns the Donatists' impious and arrogant error against the Catholic Church.
This book begins as follows: "We have already said much, we have already written much."
Chapter 62.
On the Grace of the New Testament, to Honoratus, One Book.

At the very time when we were hard pressed by the Donatists and had already begun to be pressed by the Pelagians, a friend sent me five questions from Carthage and asked me to explain them to him in writing. They were: what is meant by the cry, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"; what the apostle means when he says, "that, rooted and grounded in love, you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth"; who the five foolish virgins and the five wise ones are; what the outer darkness is; and how "The Word became flesh" is to be understood. With the heresy I mentioned above in view, a new enemy of the grace of God, I set myself a sixth question, on the grace of the New Testament. In discussing it I included an exposition of Psalm 21, at the head of which is written what the Lord cried out on the cross, the very thing my friend had asked me first to explain. In this way I resolved all five questions, not in the order in which they were set, but as each could fittingly come up in its proper place while I was discussing the grace of the New Testament.
This book begins as follows: "You have set me five questions to discuss."
Chapter 63. On the Spirit and the Letter, to Marcellinus, One Book.

The man to whom I had written the three books entitled On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, in which the baptism of infants is also carefully discussed, wrote back to me. He said he had been troubled that I had said it was possible for a human being to be without sin, if his will did not fail him and divine help assisted him, even though no one in this life ever has been, is, or will be of such perfect righteousness. He asked how I could say that something was possible when there was no example of it. Because of his question I wrote a book entitled On the Spirit and the Letter, examining the apostle's statement, "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."

In this book, as far as God helped me, I argued fiercely against the enemies of the grace of God by which the ungodly are justified. When I was dealing with the observances of the Jews, who abstain from certain foods according to the old law, I spoke of "the ceremonies of certain foods." This word is not used in the holy Scriptures. Still, it seemed suitable to me because I remembered that ceremoniae were so called from carere, "to go without," as though carimoniae, since those who observe them go without the things they abstain from. If there is some other origin of this word that is foreign to true religion, I did not use it in that sense, but in the one I have just mentioned.
This book begins as follows: "Having read the short works I recently wrote for you, my dearest son Marcellinus."
Chapter 64. On Faith and Works, One Book.

Meanwhile some brothers, laymen but devoted to the study of the divine Scriptures, sent me some writings that separated Christian faith from good works in such a way as to argue that one cannot reach eternal life without faith, but can without works. In reply I wrote a book called On Faith and Works. In it I discussed not only how those reborn by the grace of Christ ought to live, but also what kind of people should be admitted to the bath of rebirth.
This book begins as follows: "Some people think."
Chapter 65. A Summary of the Conference with the Donatists, Three Books.

After our conference with the Donatists had taken place, I briefly recounted what was done and set it down in writing according to the three days on which we met with them. I thought this would be a useful work. With its help anyone can learn without effort what happened, or, by consulting the numbers I noted beside each item, can look up whatever he wishes at its place in the proceedings themselves, since the proceedings tire the reader with their excessive length. The title of this work is A Summary of the Conference.
This work begins as follows: "When the Catholic bishops and those of the party of Donatus."
Chapter 66.
Against the Donatists after the Conference, One Book.

I also wrote a fairly long book, as I judge, carefully addressed to the Donatists themselves after the conference we held with their bishops, so that they would no longer be led astray by them. In it I also answered certain empty claims of theirs that had managed to reach us, which in their defeat they were boasting of wherever and however they could. This was in addition to what I said about the proceedings of the conference, from which what had taken place might be briefly learned. I did the same much more briefly in a further letter to them, but because at the council of Numidia all of us who were there agreed that it should be done, it is not among my letters. It begins thus: "Silvanus the senior bishop, Valentinus, Innocent, Maximinus, Optatus, Augustine, Donatus and the other bishops of the Council of Zerta, to the Donatists."
This book begins thus: "Why, Donatists, are you still being led astray?"
CHAPTER 67. ON SEEING GOD: ONE BOOK.

I wrote a book On Seeing God, in which I put off a more careful inquiry into the spiritual body that will exist at the resurrection of the saints, and whether or how God, who is spirit, is seen through such a body. Afterwards, however, I explained that question, which is truly very difficult, well enough, as I think, in the last book of The City of God, that is, the twenty-second. In a manuscript of ours that also contains this book, I also found a memorandum I wrote on this matter to Fortunatianus, bishop of Sicca. It is not entered in the list of my works, either among the books or among the letters.
This book begins thus: "Mindful of my debt"; the memorandum thus: "As I asked you in person, so now I remind you."
CHAPTER 68.
ON NATURE AND GRACE: ONE BOOK.

At that time a certain book of Pelagius also came into my hands, in which he defends human nature with every argument he could find against the grace of God, by which the ungodly are justified and by which we are Christians. I wrote a book in reply, defending grace not as something opposed to nature but as that by which nature is set free and governed, and I called it On Nature and Grace.

In it I defended certain words that Pelagius had cited as the words of Xystus, bishop of Rome and martyr, as though they really were his, for that is what I had believed. But afterwards I read that they belonged to Sextus the philosopher, not to the Christian Xystus.
This book begins thus: "The book you sent."
CHAPTER 69.
THE CITY OF GOD: TWENTY-TWO BOOKS.

Meanwhile Rome was overthrown in a great and violent disaster by the invasion of the Goths under King Alaric. The worshippers of the many false gods, whom we commonly call pagans, tried to blame its fall on the Christian religion and began to blaspheme the true God more harshly and bitterly than usual. Burning with zeal for the house of God, I therefore set out to write the books On the City of God against their blasphemies and errors. This work occupied me for several years, because many other matters kept intervening which could not be put off and had to be dealt with first. This great work on the City of God was at last completed in twenty-two books. The first five refute those who would have human affairs prosper in such a way that they think the worship of the many gods the pagans used to worship necessary for it, and who argue that these evils arise and abound because that worship is forbidden. The next five speak against those who admit that these evils have never been absent from mortals and never will be, and that they vary, now great and now small, with places, times and persons, but who argue that the worship of many gods, in which sacrifice is offered to them, is useful for the life that is to come after death. These ten books, then, refute these two empty opinions, which are hostile to the Christian religion.

But so that no one could charge us with having only refuted the views of others without stating our own, the second part of this work, which is contained in twelve books, sets about this task. Even so, where necessary we state our own views in the first ten books and refute opposing ones in the last twelve. Of the twelve books that follow, the first four contain the origin of the two cities, one of which is God's and the other this world's; the second four, their course or progress; and the third four, which are also the last, their due ends. So although all twenty-two books were written about both cities, they took their title from the better one and are called instead The City of God.

In the tenth of these books I should not have presented it as a miracle that, at Abraham's sacrifice, a flame sent from heaven passed between the divided victims, since this was shown to him in a vision.

In the seventeenth, where it is said of Samuel, "he was not of the sons of Aaron," it should rather have been said, "he was not the son of a priest." For the more lawful custom was for the sons of priests to succeed priests when they died. Samuel's father is indeed found among the sons of Aaron, but he was not a priest. Nor was he among Aaron's sons in the sense that Aaron himself begot him, but in the sense in which all of that people are called sons of Israel.
This work begins thus: "The most glorious city of God."
CHAPTER 70. TO THE PRESBYTER OROSIUS, AGAINST THE PRISCILLIANISTS: ONE BOOK.

Meanwhile, as briefly and clearly as I could, I answered an inquiry from a certain Orosius, a Spanish presbyter, about the Priscillianists and about certain opinions of Origen which the catholic faith rejects. The title of this little work is To Orosius, against the Priscillianists and Origenists. The inquiry itself is attached at the beginning of my reply.
This book begins thus: "To answer your questions, my dearest son Orosius."
CHAPTER 71.
TO THE PRESBYTER JEROME: TWO BOOKS, ONE ON THE ORIGIN OF THE SOUL AND THE OTHER ON THE SAYING OF JAMES.

I also wrote two books to the presbyter Jerome, who was living in Bethlehem, consulting him on two matters. One was on the origin of the human soul. The other was on the saying of the apostle James: "Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all." In the first I did not myself solve the question I set out. In the second, however, I did not keep silent about how I thought it should be solved, but asked whether he too agreed. He wrote back praising my inquiry, but said that he was not in a position to answer it. As long as he was still in the body, I was unwilling to publish these books, in case he might answer at some point and they could be published together with his reply. After his death, however, I published the first, so that whoever reads it may be advised either not to inquire at all how the soul is given to those being born, or at least, on so obscure a matter, to accept only a solution of this question that does not contradict the plainest truths. For the catholic faith knows, concerning original sin, that infants are without doubt condemned unless they are reborn in Christ. I published the second so that the solution we thought right for the question treated there might also be known.
This work begins thus: "Our God, who has called us."
CHAPTER 72. TO EMERITUS, BISHOP OF THE DONATISTS, AFTER THE CONFERENCE: ONE BOOK.

Some time after the conference we held with the Donatists, I wrote a book to Emeritus, their bishop, who seemed to be the chief advocate of their cause at that conference. The book is quite useful, since it gathers together, conveniently and briefly, the facts by which they are defeated, or are shown to have been defeated.
This book begins thus: "If even now, brother Emeritus."
CHAPTER 73. ON THE PROCEEDINGS OF PELAGIUS: ONE BOOK.

About the same time, in the East, that is, in Syria Palaestina, Pelagius was brought before a tribunal of bishops by certain catholic brothers. Those who had submitted the written charges against him were absent, because they could not attend on the day of the synod, and he was heard by fourteen bishops. When the doctrines hostile to the grace of Christ were read out against him from the charge sheet, he condemned them, and the bishops pronounced him catholic. When the record of these proceedings came into our hands, I wrote a book about it. Since he had been in a sense acquitted, I did not want the judges to be thought to have approved those doctrines too, for if he had not condemned them, he would certainly not have left their presence anything but condemned.
This book begins thus: "After there came into our hands."
CHAPTER 74.
ON THE CORRECTION OF THE DONATISTS: ONE BOOK.

At the same time I also wrote a book On the Correction of the Donatists for those who did not want them to be corrected by the imperial laws. This book begins thus: "I praise, I rejoice, and I admire."
CHAPTER 75.
ON THE PRESENCE OF GOD, TO DARDANUS: ONE BOOK.

I wrote a book On the Presence of God. In it my attention is chiefly on guard against the Pelagian heresy, though it is not named explicitly. But it also contains a careful and subtle discussion of the presence of the nature that we call the supreme and true God, and of his temple.
This book begins thus: "I confess, dearest brother Dardanus."
CHAPTER 76. AGAINST PELAGIUS AND CAELESTIUS, ON THE GRACE OF CHRIST AND ON ORIGINAL SIN, TO ALBINA, PINIANUS AND MELANIA: TWO BOOKS.

The Pelagian heresy and its authors were refuted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman church, first Innocent and then Zosimus, aided by letters from the African councils. After this I wrote two books against them, one On the Grace of Christ and the other On Original Sin.
This work begins thus: "How greatly we rejoice at your bodily and, above all, your spiritual well-being."
CHAPTER 77. PROCEEDINGS WITH EMERITUS THE DONATIST: ONE BOOK.

Some time after the conference we held with the Donatist heretics, we had to travel to Mauretania Caesariensis. There, in Caesarea itself, we saw Emeritus, bishop of the Donatists. He was one of the seven they had chosen to defend their cause, and the one who had worked hardest for it. What passed between us is attested by the ecclesiastical record, which is kept among my works. It took place in the presence of the bishops of that province and of the people of the church of Caesarea, the city where he was both a citizen and the bishop of the heretics in question. Unable to find any answer, he sat as if mute through my whole address, which I delivered about the Maximianists alone in his hearing and that of everyone present.

This book, or rather this record, begins thus: "IN THE CONSULSHIP OF THE MOST GLORIOUS HONORIUS AUGUSTUS FOR THE TWELFTH TIME AND CONSTANTIUS FOR THE SECOND TIME, MEN OF CLARISSIMUS RANK, ON THE ELEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF OCTOBER, AT CAESAREA, IN THE GREATER CHURCH."
CHAPTER 78.
AGAINST A SERMON OF THE ARIANS: ONE BOOK.

Meanwhile a sermon of the Arians came into my hands without the name of its author. At the urgent request of the person who had sent it to me, I answered it as briefly and quickly as I could. I attached the sermon at the beginning of my reply and numbered each point, so that by looking at the numbers one can easily see which passage each of our answers addresses.
After their sermon, which is attached at the beginning, this book begins thus: "With this discussion I answer their preceding discussion."
CHAPTER 79. ON MARRIAGE AND CONCUPISCENCE, TO VALERIUS: TWO BOOKS.

I wrote two books to the illustrious Count Valerius after hearing that the Pelagians had written something or other to him about us, namely that we condemned marriage by asserting original sin. The title of these books is On Marriage and Concupiscence. For we defended the goodness of marriage, so that the concupiscence of the flesh and the law in the members that wars against the law of the mind would not be thought a fault of marriage. Conjugal chastity makes good use of this evil of lust for the procreation of children. There came to be two books in the following way. The first came into the hands of Julian the Pelagian, and he wrote four books against it. Someone copied out a few passages from these and sent them to Count Valerius, who sent them on to us. When I received them, I answered those very passages in another book.
The first book of this work begins thus: "New heretics, dearest son Valerius"; the second thus: "Amid the cares of your military service."
CHAPTER 80.
EXPRESSIONS: SEVEN BOOKS.

I produced seven books on seven books of the divine scriptures, namely the five books of Moses, the one of Joshua son of Nun, and the one of Judges. In them I noted the expressions in each that are less usual in our language. Readers who pay too little attention to these look for a hidden meaning in the divine words when it is merely a way of speaking. Sometimes they extract something that is not, indeed, at odds with the truth, yet the author who wrote it is not found to have meant it; it seems more likely that he said it simply as a way of speaking. Many obscure things in the holy scriptures become clear once the way of speaking is recognized. For this reason these ways of speaking should be learned where the meaning is plain, so that where it is hidden this very knowledge may come to our aid and open the meaning to the attentive mind. The title of this work is Expressions in Genesis, and so on for each of the books.

In the first book I set down that it is written, "And Noah did all the words that the Lord commanded him; so he did," and I said this expression was like the one in the account of creation where, after the words "And so it was done," the words "And God made" are added. This does not now seem to me entirely similar. For there a meaning also lies hidden, whereas here there is only a way of speaking.
This work begins thus: "The expressions of the scriptures."
CHAPTER 81. QUESTIONS: SEVEN BOOKS.

At the same time I also wrote books of Questions on the same seven divine books. I chose to call them this because I put forward the matters discussed in them as things to be inquired into rather than as inquiries already resolved. Even so, many more of them seem to me to have been treated thoroughly enough that they could fairly be judged resolved and explained. We had also begun to examine the books of Kingdoms in the same way, but before we had gone far we turned our attention to other, more pressing matters.

In the first book there is a discussion of the streaked rods that Jacob placed in the water, so that the ewes, when they conceived, would see them as they drank and bear streaked young. There we did not explain well why he did not set them out when the ewes conceived a second time, that is, when they conceived other young, but only at the first conception. For the explanation of another question, where it is asked why Jacob said to his father-in-law, "You have cheated me of my wages by ten lambs," is worked out quite truly, and it shows that this one was not solved as it should have been.

Also in the third book there is a discussion of the high priest and how he could beget children. He had to enter the holy of holies, where the altar of incense was, twice a day to offer incense morning and evening, and, as the law says, no one unclean could enter. Yet the same law says that a man becomes unclean even through conjugal intercourse; it commands him to wash with water, but says that even after washing he is unclean until evening. From this I said it followed that either he remained continent or the incense was left off on some days. I did not see that this did not follow. For the words "He shall be unclean until evening" can be understood to mean that he was unclean only up to the evening and no longer unclean once evening came. In that case he could offer incense clean at the evening hour, having lain with his wife after the morning incense in order to beget children.

Likewise, it was asked how the high priest could be forbidden to go in to the body of his dead father, since there was only one high priest at a time and the son was not supposed to be made priest until his priestly father had died. I said that it must therefore have been necessary for the son to be appointed to succeed his father immediately after his death, before the father was buried, so that the incense, which had to be offered twice a day, would also continue without a break. That priest, then, is forbidden to go in to the body of his father, who is not yet buried. But I paid too little attention to the possibility that this command was given rather because of those who would become high priests without succeeding a father who was high priest, yet were still among the sons, that is, the descendants, of Aaron. This could happen if a high priest either had no sons or had sons so reprobate that none of them ought to succeed their father. So it was that Samuel succeeded the high priest Eli: he was not himself the son of a priest, but he was nonetheless one of the sons, that is, the descendants, of Aaron.

Also, concerning the thief to whom it was said, "Today you will be with me in paradise," I stated as if it were certain that he had not been visibly baptized. Yet this is uncertain, and it should rather be believed that he was baptized, as I myself argued later elsewhere.

Likewise, in the fifth book, where the mothers named in the gospel genealogies are discussed, I said that they are listed only together with the fathers. That is indeed true, but it has nothing to do with the matter under discussion. The discussion concerned men who married the wives of brothers or kinsmen who had died without sons, on account of Joseph's two fathers, one named by Matthew and the other by Luke. I discussed this question carefully in this work when we were reviewing our work Against Faustus the Manichaean.
This work begins thus: "Since the holy scriptures that are called canonical."
CHAPTER 82. ON THE SOUL AND ITS ORIGIN: FOUR BOOKS.

At the same time a certain Vincentius Victor, in Mauretania Caesariensis, came across a little work of mine in the possession of a Spanish presbyter named Peter. In one passage of it I admitted that I did not know the origin of the soul of each individual human being: whether souls are propagated from the soul of the first man and thereafter from parents, or whether, as with that first man, each one is given to each person without any propagation. I said, however, that I did know the soul is not a body but a spirit. Against these statements of mine he wrote two books addressed to this same Peter, and the monk Renatus sent them to me from Caesarea. After reading them, I wrote four books in reply: one to the monk Renatus, another to the presbyter Peter, and two to Victor himself. The one to Peter, although it is as long as a book, is really a letter, but I did not want to separate it from the other three. In all of them many necessary matters are discussed. I defended my hesitation about the origin of the souls given to individual human beings, and I exposed the many errors and perversities of his presumption. Yet I dealt with him as gently as I could, as a young man not to be hastily condemned but still to be taught, and I received from him a written statement of his correction.

The book of this work addressed to Renatus begins thus: "Your sincerity toward us"; the one to Peter thus: "To my most beloved lord, father and fellow presbyter Peter"; and of the last two, addressed to Vincentius Victor, the first begins thus: "What I thought I should write to you."
CHAPTER 83.
TO POLLENTIUS, ON ADULTEROUS MARRIAGES: TWO BOOKS.

I wrote two books on adulterous marriages, seeking to resolve a very difficult question as far as I could in accordance with the scriptures. Whether I did so with complete clarity I do not know. Indeed, I feel that I have not dealt with this matter completely, although I have opened up many of its hidden corners, as anyone who reads with understanding will be able to judge.
The first book of this work begins thus: "The first question, dearest brother Pollentius"; the second thus: "Regarding what you had written to me."
CHAPTER 84. AGAINST AN ADVERSARY OF THE LAW AND THE PROPHETS: TWO BOOKS.

Meanwhile a book by some heretic was being read aloud in the square by the harbor at Carthage, before large crowds who listened very attentively. The author was either a Marcionite or one of those whose error holds that God did not make this world, and that the God of the law given through Moses, and of the prophets connected with that law, is not the true God but a most wicked demon. Some brothers, very earnest Christians, got hold of the book and sent it to me without delay to refute, urgently asking that I too not delay my reply. I refuted it in two books, which I entitled Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets because the manuscript that was sent did not bear its author's name.
This work begins thus: "To the book you sent, dearest brothers."
CHAPTER 85.
AGAINST GAUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF THE DONATISTS: TWO BOOKS.

About the same time Dulcitius, a tribune and notary, was here in Africa enforcing the imperial decrees issued against the Donatists. He sent a letter to Gaudentius of Thamugadi, the Donatist bishop, who had been one of the seven they chose to conduct their defense at our conference. Gaudentius was threatening to set fire to the church he was in and burn himself and his people to death in it. Dulcitius urged him to embrace catholic unity and tried to dissuade him from the burning. He also added that if they thought themselves righteous, they should flee, according to the precept of the Lord Christ, rather than burn themselves in wicked fires. Gaudentius wrote back two letters. One was short, because, as he claimed, the courier was in a hurry. The other was long, as if replying more fully and carefully. The tribune I mentioned thought they should be sent to me, so that I could refute them myself. I refuted both of them in a single book. When this came into Gaudentius's hands, he wrote back to me whatever he saw fit, answering with no reasoning at all, but rather showing that he could neither answer nor keep silent. This could be clear enough to those who read intelligently and compare our statements with his. Still, I did not want to leave it unanswered, whatever it was. So it came about that there are these two books of ours addressed to him.
This work begins thus: "Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Thamugadi."
CHAPTER 86. AGAINST LYING: ONE BOOK.

At that time I also wrote a book Against Lying. The occasion for this work was that some Catholics thought they ought to pretend to be Priscillianists in order to get into their hiding places and track down the Priscillianist heretics, who believe they should conceal their heresy not only by denial but even by lying. I wrote this book to forbid this.
This book begins as follows: "You have sent me a great deal to read."
CHAPTER 87
AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF THE PELAGIANS, IN FOUR BOOKS

Next come four books that I wrote against two letters of the Pelagians, addressed to Boniface, bishop of the Roman church. When these letters had come into his hands he sent them to me himself, having found my name inserted in them slanderously.
This work begins as follows: "I had indeed already known you through your widely celebrated reputation."
CHAPTER 88
AGAINST JULIAN, IN SIX BOOKS

Meanwhile the four books of Julian the Pelagian that I mentioned above also came into my hands. In them I found that the passages excerpted by the person who had sent them to Count Valerius had not all been written to the count exactly as Julian had stated them; some had been altered to a certain extent. So I wrote six books against those four. The first two of mine refute Julian's impudence with the testimonies of the saints who defended the Catholic faith after the apostles. He thought he could charge us with a Manichaean doctrine because we say that original sin is derived from Adam, and that it is removed by the washing of regeneration not only in adults but also in little children. In the latter part of my first book I showed how much Julian himself assists the Manichaeans through some of his own statements. My remaining four books answer his four, one by one.

In the fifth volume of this long and carefully worked-out work, however, where I mentioned that an ugly husband used to set a beautiful picture before his wife during intercourse so that she would not bear ugly children, I gave the man's name as though it were certain, when in fact it is uncertain, because my memory deceived me. Soranus, the medical writer, wrote that a king of Cyprus used to do this, but he did not give his personal name.
This work begins as follows: "Your insults and abusive words, Julian."
CHAPTER 89
ON FAITH, HOPE, AND LOVE, IN ONE BOOK

I also wrote a book On Faith, Hope, and Love, when the person to whom it is addressed had asked me for a little work of mine that he could keep always in his hands, the kind of thing the Greeks call an enchiridion, a handbook. In it I think I have covered quite carefully how God is to be worshiped, which divine scripture defines as the true wisdom of a human being.
This book begins as follows: "I cannot say, my dearest son Laurence, how much your learning delights me."
CHAPTER 90
ON THE CARE TO BE TAKEN FOR THE DEAD, TO BISHOP PAULINUS, IN ONE BOOK
I wrote the book On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead after I had been asked by letter whether it benefits anyone after death that his body is buried near the shrine of some saint.
This book begins as follows: "To your Holiness, venerable fellow bishop Paulinus."
CHAPTER 91. ON EIGHT QUESTIONS OF DULCITIUS, IN ONE BOOK

The book I have entitled On Eight Questions of Dulcitius would not need to be mentioned in this work among my books, since it is made up of material I had previously written in other works, were it not that some discussion added by me is also found in it, and that to one of those questions I gave an answer taken not from some earlier work of mine but whatever could occur to me at the time.
This book begins as follows: "As it seems to me, my dearest son Dulcitius."
CHAPTER 92. TO VALENTINUS AND THE MONKS WITH HIM: ON GRACE AND FREE WILL, IN ONE BOOK

Because of those who think free will is being denied when the grace of God is defended, and who therefore defend free will in such a way as to deny the grace of God, claiming that it is given according to our merits, I wrote a book entitled On Grace and Free Will. I wrote it to the monks of Hadrumetum, in whose monastery a dispute had begun over this matter, so that some of them felt compelled to consult me.
This book begins as follows: "Because of those who [defend] human free will"
CHAPTER 93
TO THE SAME PERSONS AS ABOVE: ON REBUKE AND GRACE, IN ONE BOOK

I wrote another book to the same monks, which I have entitled On Rebuke and Grace, when it was reported to me that someone there had said that no one ought to be rebuked if he does not keep God's commandments, but that we should only pray for him that he may keep them.
This book begins as follows: "Having read your letter, Valentinus, dearest brother."

When I made this review, I recalled that I had dictated these ninety-three works in two hundred and thirty-two books. I do not know whether I am yet to dictate any more. At the urging of the brothers I published this review of them in two books before I had begun to review my letters and my sermons to the people, the former dictated and the latter preached by me.
